O R D E R
1. These  petitions  for  contempt  have  been  presented  before  this  Court
during 2024 – 2026 alleging deliberate and wilful violation of interim orders
passed on diverse dates by this Court during 2014-2015 in Civil Appeal Nos.
4347-4375 of 2014.
2. We have had the occasion to look into the final order of disposal of such
appeals by the order dated 25 th July, 2017, reported in (2018) 12 SCC 595.
Operative part of the order reads as follows:
“19. Vide interim order dated 25-3-2014 1; this Court directed
the State of Uțtar Pradesh to fill up the vacancies of Assistant
Teachers  in  terms  of  the  impugned  judgment 2.  Thereafter,  on
17.12.20143,  the  said  order  was  modified  and  the  State  was
directed to appoint candidates whose names were not involved in
malpractices in the TET test and who had obtained 70% marks
(65% for SC, ST, OBC and physically handicapped or any other
category covered by the government policy for reservation). 54,464
posts have already been filled up in compliance with the orders of
this Court. The said appointments were subject to result of these
matters.  It  was  also  observed  that  if  anyone  without  TET
1  Ram Prakash Sharma vs. State of U.P., (2015) 17 SCC 230
2  Shiv Kumar Pathak vs. State of U.P., 2013 SCC OnLine All 11012; (2013) 10 ADJ 121
3  State of U.P. vs. Shiv Kumar Pathak, (2014)15 SCC 606: (2015) 3 SCC (L&S) 664

--- Page 24 ---
3
qualification is appointed his services will be terminated. Vide order
dated 2-11-20154 it was noted that against 72,825 posts which were
advertised, 43,077 candidates had completed training and were
working while 15,058 candidates were undergoing training. Around
14,690 posts were vacant. It was further observed that candidates
who had the required percentage of marks in terms of order dated
27-7-2015  were  to  file  their  applications  and  a  Committee
constituted for the said purpose could verify such percentage and if
parity was found the same benefit could be extended.
20. We have been informed that 66,655 teachers have already
been appointed in pursuance of the interim orders of this Court.
Having regard to the entirety of circumstances, we are not inclined
to disturb the same. We make it clear that the State is at liberty to
fill up the remaining vacancies in accordance with law after issuing
a fresh advertisement.”
3. It is clear from the aforesaid extract that this Court did not disturb the
appointments already made, although it could be so (as contended by the
petitioners)  that  some  of  the  appointees  being  ineligible  did  not  deserve
appointment in the first place and that it is they (the petitioners) who should
have been appointed as per the interim orders.
4. In our opinion, these contentions should have been raised before this
Court prior to disposal of the said civil appeals by the order dated 25 th July,
2017.  We are informed that the contentions were raised; however, nothing
turns  on  such  submission.   In  the  absence  of  a  positive  direction  for
appointment of the petitioners in the remaining vacancies (which, as per the
said order,  the State was free to fill up by issuing a fresh advertisement), as
well as the fact that review petition(s) were dismissed, we are unable to accept
that  there  has  been  any  disobedience  of  this  Court’s  order,   much  less
contempt.
4  State of U.P. vs. Shiv Kumar Pathak, (2015) 17 SCC 230 : (2015) 17 SCC 238

--- Page 25 ---
4
5. In view of final disposal of the civil appeals by the aforesaid order, the
interim orders have merged in such final order. Contempt has been alleged of
interim  orders  which  have  no  independent  existence,  beyond  the  date  of
disposal of the civil appeals. Question of entertaining contempt petitions against
such interim orders, which do not exist, does not and cannot arise.
6. The  petitions,  alleging  contempt  of  interim  orders,  are  wholly
misconceived and not maintainable; hence, the same are dismissed.
7. Pending  interlocutory  application(s)  including  application(s)  for
intervention / impleadment, if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. Hon’ble Mr. Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha pronounced the
judgment of the Bench comprising His Lordship and  Hon’ble Mr.
Justice Alok Aradhe.
2. Permission to file Civil Appeal/Special Leave Petition is/are
19 of 42

--- Page 87 ---
granted. 
3. Leave granted in Special Leave Petitions.
4. The present batch of matters stands dismissed in terms of the
signed reportable judgment. Paragraph nos. 39 to 41 of the Judgment
read as under:-
“39.  Having considered the matter in detail, we
are of the opinion that, 
i) No case for interference in the present
Special Leave Petitions/Civil Appeals is made
out.  They  are  accordingly  dismissed  on  the
grounds of delay as well as on merits. 
ii) We find considerable force in the submission
made by the Ld. AG that the opinion of the
Medical Board deserves to be given due weight and
ought not to be substituted by a Court merely
because another view is possible. In pending
matters, the Tribunal must scrutinize in detail
the opinion and reasons expressed by the Medical
Board before deciding upon the claims.
iii) If a claimant approaches the relevant
forum  after  a  period  of  fifteen  years,  the
principle in Rule 7 of the Entitlement Rules 2008
applies and the burden shifts. Onus in such a
case will be on the applicant to prove the
conditions of entitlement.
40. With  the  clarification  as  indicated
hereinabove, the present batch of matters stands
dismissed.
41. There shall be no order as to costs.”
5.    Diary No. 49040 of 2025 and Writ petition (C) No. 1067 of
2025 are de-tagged from the present batch of matters. 
6. After pronouncement of judgment, Ms. Archana Pathak Dave,
learned Additional Solicitor General prays that some time may be
granted to them to comply with the directions in the orders
impugned in these matters, which have been upheld by us. 
7. At the request of learned Additional Solicitor General,
20 of 42

--- Page 88 ---
four months' time is granted to the Union of India to comply with
the directions in the orders impugned in these batch of matters.
8.  Pending  application(s),  including  application(s)  for
intervention stand disposed of.

1. Hon’ble Mr. Justice Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha pronounced the
judgment of the Bench comprising His Lordship and  Hon’ble Mr.
Justice Alok Aradhe.
2. Permission to file Civil Appeal/Special Leave Petition is/are
granted. 
3. Leave granted in Special Leave Petitions.
40 of 42

--- Page 108 ---
4. The present batch of matters stands dismissed in terms of the
signed reportable judgment. Paragraph nos. 39 to 41 of the Judgment
read as under:-
“39.  Having considered the matter in detail, we
are of the opinion that, 
i) No case for interference in the present
Special Leave Petitions/Civil Appeals is made
out.  They  are  accordingly  dismissed  on  the
grounds of delay as well as on merits. 
ii) We find considerable force in the submission
made by the Ld. AG that the opinion of the
Medical Board deserves to be given due weight and
ought not to be substituted by a Court merely
because another view is possible. In pending
matters, the Tribunal must scrutinize in detail
the opinion and reasons expressed by the Medical
Board before deciding upon the claims.
iii) If a claimant approaches the relevant
forum  after  a  period  of  fifteen  years,  the
principle in Rule 7 of the Entitlement Rules 2008
applies and the burden shifts. Onus in such a
case will be on the applicant to prove the
conditions of entitlement.
40. With  the  clarification  as  indicated
hereinabove, the present batch of matters stands
dismissed.
41. There shall be no order as to costs.”
5.    Diary No. 49040 of 2025 and Writ petition (C) No. 1067 of
2025 are de-tagged from the present batch of matters. 
6. After pronouncement of judgment, Ms. Archana Pathak Dave,
learned Additional Solicitor General prays that some time may be
granted to them to comply with the directions in the orders
impugned in these matters, which have been upheld by us. 
7. At the request of learned Additional Solicitor General,
four months' time is granted to the Union of India to comply with
the directions in the orders impugned in these batch of matters.

intervention stand disposed of.

                                VERSUS
MALLIKARJUN & ORS.                               RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
C.A. NO.2844 OF 2011:
Delay in filing substitution application is condoned.
Abatement is set aside. Application for substitution to bring
on record the legal representatives of deceased-respondent
no.4 is allowed. 
Application for intervention is allowed. 
The question of law involved in this appeal has been
settled  by  a  larger  Bench  decision  of  this  Court  in
‘Revanasiddappa & Anr Vs Mallikarjun & Ors.’, reported in 2023
SCC ONLINE SC 1087. 
In  such  view  of  the  matter,  nothing  survives  for
consideration in this appeal. However, the parties are at
liberty to seek a further preliminary decree as the respondent
No.4 is no more. If such an application is filed, the same has
to be decided on its own merits and in accordance with law, as

--- Page 151 ---
2
law does not prohibit successive preliminary decree by taking
into consideration the subsequent development of facts and
law. 
The appeal stands disposed of in the above terms. 
Pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed of.
C.A. No. 7318/2014:
Heard learned counsel for the appellants.
Despite notice being served and the name of the counsel
appearing in the cause list, none appears on behalf of the
respondents.
A short question that arises for consideration is as to
whether the appellants being the illegitimate children born
out of the relation between Hira Lal (deceased) and Sarti @
Manbhari  are  entitled  for  appropriate  shares  of  the
properties.  The Courts below held that the appellant being
the illegitimate children of the deceased Hira Lal it is only
his brother Mangla and others who are entitled to their
respective shares and not the appellants.
Learned counsel appearing for the appellants submits that
the issue involved has been settled by the larger Bench
decision of this Court in ‘Revanasiddappa & Anr Vs Mallikarjun
& Ors.’, reported in 2023 SCC ONLINE SC 1087, where the rights
of the illegitimate children over the property of the father
is covered.  We find force in the aforesaid contention raised.

--- Page 152 ---
3
In view of the aforesaid pronouncement of law by the
larger Bench of this Court in the judgment referred to in
‘Revanasiddappa’ (supra), the impugned judgment confirming the
judgment of the Trial Court stands set aside and the matter is
remitted  back  to  the  Trial  Court  for  passing  a  fresh
preliminary decree.  
The appeal stands allowed and the Trial Court is directed
to pass a fresh preliminary decree by taking note of the law
laid down in ‘Revanasiddappa’ (supra).
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
C.A. No. 4398/2019 :
The issue raised in this appeal is covered by the larger
Bench decision of this Court in  ‘Revanasiddappa & Anr Vs
Mallikarjun & Ors.’, reported in 2023 SCC ONLINE SC 1087.
In such view of the matter the appeal stands disposed of.
However,  it  is  well  open  to  the  parties  including  the
appellants  to  exercise  their  remedy  by  seeking  another
preliminary decree in terms of the judgment aforementioned.
The appeal is disposed of accordingly.
C.A. No        @ SLP (C) No.1573-1574/2021:
Leave granted.
The only question to be considered in this appeal is as

--- Page 153 ---
4
to whether the appellant nos. 2 to 5 being the illegitimate
children of the first appellant are entitled for any share in
the suit properties or not.  As already been decided by this
Court hereinabove in ‘ Revanasiddappa & Anr Vs Mallikarjun &
Ors.’, reported in 2023 SCC ONLINE SC 1087 to the effect that
an illegitimate child is entitled for a share in the property
allotted to the father.  
In  such  view  of  the  matter  nothing  survives  for
consideration, while making it clear that it is always open to
the first appellant to deal with his share as he likes and in
the event of his death, the shares of the remaining appellants
can be worked out.
The appeals are disposed of in the above terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Interlocutory Application No.204507 of 2026 is dismissed, as
not pressed. 
2. We heard Mr. Shyam Divan, the learned Amicus and all other
learned counsel appearing in this litigation.
3. In the course of today’s hearing, we first looked into the
Status Report forwarded by the MPID Court, i.e., the designated
Special Judge (under MPID Act) and Additional Sessions Judge, City
Civil and Sessions Court, Greater Mumbai (CR 20).
4. We are disappointed reading the Status Report forwarded by the
learned Presiding Officer.
5. It appears that there is no progress at all insofar as the
Special Case No.19 of 2018 is concerned.
6. We take notice of the fact that charge-sheet was filed way
back on 25.09.2018. In this particular charge-sheet, four companies
and four individuals have been arrayed as accused. All accused are
on bail.
7. It  is  very  disturbing  to  note  that  between  2018  and
13.09.2022, the trial got adjourned only for the purpose of
appearance of the accused persons. These accused persons are none
other but members of one particular family.
8. The Report indicates that accused nos. 4 to 8 remained absent
and kept on praying for exemption from personal appearance. Accused
6

--- Page 172 ---
no.7, namely, Suchita Omprakash Goyanka sought permission to travel
abroad on five to seven occasions. She preferred a discharge
application  under  Section  239  of  the  Cr.P.C.  on  09.04.2025.
Ultimately, the discharge application was finally heard and has
been rejected vide order dated 09.09.2026.
9. We also take notice of the fact that a supplementary charge-
sheet came to be filed by the EOW on 18.02.2026. This supplementary
charge-sheet has been filed against the accused nos. 9 to 11,
respectively and accused no.12- company.
10. Thus, now, in all, 12 accused are to be put to trial.
11. We also take notice of the fact that after the supplementary
charge-sheet came to be filed, the court concerned issued summons
to the newly added accused nos. 9 to 12, respectively. It took two
months for the I.O. to serve summons on accused nos. 10 and 11,
respectively by e-mail.
12. We take serious notice of the fact that accused nos. 10 and 11
are sitting fine in Dubai. They are not appearing before the Trial
Court.
13. We direct the Trial Court to now proceed to issue non-bailable
warrants, including lookout notice and secure their presence at the
earliest at any cost. It will be now be the sole responsibility of
the Trial Court concerned to act accordingly. Failure to respond to
the warrants shall entail the consequences of proclamation.
14. We direct all other accused persons to appear before the Trial
Court for the purpose of framing of charge.
15. We direct the Trial Court to ensure at any cost, that the
charge is framed within a period of eight (08) weeks from today.
7

--- Page 173 ---
16. If there is no cooperation at the end of any of the accused
persons, stern steps shall be taken as directed by us.
17. If any accused person intends to file a discharge application,
the same shall be filed within a period of one week from today and,
thereafter, no discharge application shall be entertained.
18. We, thereafter, looked into the application filed by SEBI.
19. SEBI in its application, i.e., I.A. No.280210/2026 has prayed
for the following:-
“ (a)Allow the present application of the Respondent SEBI
in the captioned Civil Appeal and grant additional 6
months time from October 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027 to the
A.P. Kurhekar Committee for making refund process and
consequential activities to the investors and to submit
compliance report, and 
(b) Pass such other and further order/ orders as this
Hon’ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case may also be passed.”
20. We heard Mr. Bhargava V. Desai, the learned counsel appearing
for SEBI. We are inclined to grant six months’ time from 01 st
October, 2026 till 31 st March, 2027 to the A.P. Kurhekar Committee
for making refund process and consequential activities to the
investors  and  to  submit  a  compliance  report  thereafter.  We,
accordingly grant the time as prayed for.
21. We, thereafter, took up the Report filed by the Directorate of
Enforcement. We heard Mr. N. Venkataraman, the learned A.S.G.
appearing for the Directorate of Enforcement.
22. This Status Report has been filed in pursuance of our order
dated 23.04.2026. The Report highlights the background of the case
8

--- Page 174 ---
in brief leading to proceedings under the PMLA, the investigation
undertaken under the PMLA and other details.
23. The  Report  highlights  something  very  serious.  The  PMLA
investigation so far has revealed that out of the gross collection
of Rs.8,852 crore received in cash and partly through cheques,
Rs.3,430 crore was repaid/ refunded to various investors while
Rs.3,077 crore was paid to the agents as commission/ incentives at
the exorbitant rate of 27% to 39%. The Report further states that
Rs.1,723 crore were transferred to associates/ sister concerns
ostensibly for the purchase of assets, acquisition of equity in
associates companies, etc.
24. It appears that properties have been purchased in Dubai,
including a restaurant, etc. The Report states that the identified
assets of hundreds of crores will be provisionally attached under
the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002,
wherever  found  to  be  involved  in  money  laundering.  The
investigation seems to be in progress.
25. We are of the view that it is high time that the ED now
proceeds to take further steps in the form of filing complaint,
etc., in accordance with law.
26. We request Mr. N. Venkataraman, the learned A.S.G. to ensure
that appropriate further steps are taken in the right direction and
there is some further progress at the end of the ED.
27. By the next date of hearing, a further report shall be placed
on record, highlighting further developments in the matter.
28. We also heard Mr. Anshin Desai, the learned senior counsel
appearing for the applicant of I.A. No.35672/2023. The applicant,
9

--- Page 175 ---
herein is aggrieved by the action of the R.P. in including one of
his properties in the tender document dated 29.10.2021.
29. According to the learned senior counsel, in this regard, he
has lodged his objections with the Justice Deodhar Committee as
well as the RP. On the other hand, the learned Amicus would submit
that the property which the applicant is talking about was ordered
to be attached by this Court and in pursuance of such order, the
property has been attached.
30. There is no clarity in this regard. We want some further
information to be placed before us before we proceed to pass
further appropriate orders.
31. We request the learned Amicus to take further instructions in
the matter and file an appropriate Report in this regard.
32. The Resolution Professional shall also assist this Court in
this regard by filing an appropriate Report.
33. Insofar as all other interlocutory applications preferred by
different Banks are concerned, we shall look into those on the next
date of hearing.
34. Mr. Gopal Jain, the learned senior counsel has something to
say as regards the Axis Bank. According to him, one of the
properties over which Axis Bank has a first charge/ secured
interest has been put to auction. He wants that the amount fetched
in that auction should come to an escrow account of the Axis Bank.
35. There  is  no  clarity  as  regards  when  this  auction  was
undertaken, what is the amount fetched and where is this amount at
present.
36. We request the learned Amicus to assist us in this regard on
10

--- Page 176 ---
the next date of hearing.
37. We also heard Mr. Nakul Dewan, the learned senior counsel
appearing for the applicant in I.A. No.102331/2026. In this regard,
it appears that the Justice Deodhar Committee has granted its
approval insofar as the proposal put forward by the client of Mr.
Nakul Dewan is concerned.
38. This proposal has something to do with purchase of the
minority 38.20% shares in a company called Luxora Infrastructure
Private Limited for a total consideration of Rs.15,00,00,000/-
(Rupees Fifteen crore).
39. In this regard, the learned Amicus would submit that the
Deodhar Committee has referred this issue to this Court for our
consideration.
40. The learned counsel appearing for the SEBI would submit that
SEBI proposes to get the shareholding valued appropriately.
41. We give one last opportunity to the SEBI to undertake this
exercise and whatever valuation they arrived at, shall be informed
to the applicant in writing.
42. We shall take up this issue also on the next date of hearing.
43. Let this exercise be completed within a period of four weeks
from today.
44. The Status Report filed by SEBI is ordered to be taken on
record.
45. List on 27th November, 2026 at 02:00 P.M..

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No.199419/2025
1. This interlocutory application was disposed of by this Court
vide order dated 08.09.2026, in the following terms:
“1. Since the core issue that requires determination
is whether the subject leased land is revenue land or
forest area, and vide Order dated 13.11.2019, such an
issue has been remanded by this Court for adjudication
to Karnataka High Court; this application is disposed
of with a request to the High Court to take up the
pending issue and make an endeavour to decide the same,
preferably  within  three  months.  The  application
accordingly stands disposed of.”
2. Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel and Amicus Curiae, has
submitted a note to recall/modify the afore-stated order,  inter
alia, pointing out that the question as to whether the subject land
is ‘revenue land’ or ‘forest land’ has already been authoritatively
determined by a Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court vide
judgment dated 13.03.2020 passed in Writ Petition No. 29328 of 2018
(Sri B.R. Ganapathi Singh  v. State of Karnataka ).  He has further
8

--- Page 185 ---
pointed out that SLP (Civil) No. 946/2021, preferred by the
petitioner against the dismissal of his writ petition, was also
rejected by this Court vide order dated 16.11.2021.
3. It further appears that the following four writ petitions are
still pending in the Karnataka High Court, where we are informed
that the same question, namely, whether the disputed land is
‘revenue land’ or ‘forest land’ arises for consideration:
(i) W.P. No. 4254/2021
(ii) W.P. No. 29336/2018
(iii) W.P. No. 33051/2018
(iv) W.P. No. 33820/2018
4. We, thus, dispose of the instant application with a request to
Hon’ble the Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court to list the
afore-stated writ petitions for hearing before an appropriate
Bench, especially in light of the decision dated 13.03.2020 of the
High Court in B.R. Ganapathi Singh's case (supra) and to dispose of
the same at the earliest.
5. It is, however, clarified that we have not expressed any
opinion on the merits of the case.
Main Matter(s)
6. In deference to our order dated 08.09.2026, the CEC has
submitted Report No. 26 of 2026 on 28.09.2026.  Learned Senior
Counsel for the State of Karnataka is granted two weeks’ time to
file their objections, if any.
9

--- Page 186 ---
7. Similarly, learned Senior Counsel for the other affected
parties also seek and are granted two weeks' time to file their
respective objections against the said report.
8. Post these matters on 29.10.2026 at 2 p.m. for consideration
of those objections, as well as for taking up the cases that fall
under Categories II and IV onwards, as per the categorization
mentioned in paragraph 2 of this Court’s order dated 08.09.2026.
9. I.A. No.205913/2025, I.A. No.253645/2025, I.A. No.236242/2024
and I.A. No.131439/2025 (in SLP (Civil) Nos. 3585-3586/2024) and
I.A. No.13066/2026 and I.A. No.13069/2026 shall also be listed on
the next date of hearing.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026  
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No(s).1498 of 2026) 
 
 
SANJEEV KUMAR       ….APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
STATE OF PUNJAB AND ANOTHER 
….RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Heard. 
2. Leave granted.  
3. The instant appeal by special leave  has been 
filed by the appellant assailing the order dated 15 th 
December, 2025 passed by the High Court of Punjab 
and Haryana at Chandigarh1 in CRM-M No. 67293 of 
2025, rejecting the prayer made by the appellant for 
quashing of the order dated 11 th October, 2013 
passed by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, 
 
1 For short, “the High Court” 

--- Page 206 ---
2 
 
Anandpur Sahib, declaring him a proclaimed 
offender in FIR No.66 dated 07 th July, 2012 , 
registered at Police Station Nangal, District 
Rupnagar, Punjab for the offences punishable under 
Sections 406 and 498 -A of the I ndian Penal Code, 
18602.  
4. The appellant and the respondent no.2 were 
married in the year 2011 .  Soon  after the marriage, 
the relations between the parents of the appellant 
and the respondent no.2 became strained and 
accordingly the spouses started leaving separately in 
a rented accommodation.  A male child was born from 
the wedlock on 31 st October, 2011, who is presently 
in the care and custody of the respondent no.2.  
5. The respondent no.2 lodged a complaint on 08th 
June, 2012 alleging that the appellant and his 
parents had harassed, humiliated and tortured her 
on account of the demand of dowry. Based on the 
aforesaid complaint, FIR NO.66 dated 07th July, 2012 
came to be registered for the aforesaid offences.  
6. The appellant applied for pre -arrest bail in 
connection with the said FIR, however, such 
 
2 For short, “IPC” 

--- Page 207 ---
3 
 
applications were rejected right up to the High Court. 
The appellant, in the meantime, relocated to Dubai 
and has been reportedly staying there since the year 
2013.  The non-bailable warrants issued against the 
appellant were returned unexecuted with the report 
that he could not be found at the address given. As 
the appellant was not cooperating in  the tria l, 
proceedings under Section 82 and 83 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 19733 were initiated against him 
and a proclamation declaring the appellant to be an 
offender was also issued.  
7. Being aggrieved, the appellant approached the 
High Court  seeking quashing of the order of 
proclamation and the issuance of the warrants of 
arrest.  The said petition has been rejected by the 
High Court by order dated 15 th December, 2025, 
which is the subject matter of challenge in the instant 
appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the 
Constitution of India.  
8. This Court is apprised that  in the intervening 
period, the marriage between the parties has been  
dissolved by virtue of an ex parte decree of divorce 
 
3 For short, “CrPC” 

--- Page 208 ---
4 
 
granted in an application filed by the respondent 
no.2. 
9. While entertaining this appeal, this Court 
passed an order on 02nd February, 2026 directing the 
counsel for the appellant to take instructions as to 
whether the appellant was ready and willing to 
deposit a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs 
Only) to show his bona fides towards the 
maintenance of respondent no.2 and the minor son 
of the parties .  In compliance, the appellant 
expressed his readiness and willingness which has 
been recorded in the order dated 13th February, 2026.  
The appellant agreed to deposit the said amount in 
two instalments of Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs 
Only) each.  Recording the aforesaid submission of 
the appellant, the proceedings arising out of 
aforementioned FIR were stayed. 
10. On 3 rd August, 2026, when the matter was 
taken up by this Court, the Court was apprised that 
the parties have arrived at a consensus and have 
agreed to resolve all the disputes on the condition 
that the appellant would pay a sum of 
Rs.15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakhs Only) in all as 
a full and final  settlement of all claims of the 

--- Page 209 ---
5 
 
respondent and the minor son.  As against th is 
settled amount, Rs.10,00,000/- (Rupees Ten Lakhs 
Only) had already been paid to the respondent no.2 
and the remaining Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs 
Only) would be paid within one month.   
11. Today, during the course of arguments, this 
Court has been apprised that as a matter of fact, the 
appellant deposited two demand drafts for a sum of 
Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs Only) each in the 
registry of this Court which have been invested in 
separate FDRs renewed over a period of time , and 
that the amount has not been released to respondent 
no.2.  Furthermore, today the learned counsel for the 
appellant has presented a demand draft for a sum of 
Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs Only) drawn in the 
name of the Registrar, Supreme Court  of India. The 
said demand draft shall be deposited in the Registry 
forthwith.  
12. As agreed between the parties and in terms of 
the amicable settlement, out of the said amount of 
Rs.15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakhs Only) and the 
interest accrued thereupon, a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- 
(Rupees Ten Lakhs Only) shall be transferred to the 
account of the son and the remaining amount of 

--- Page 210 ---
6 
 
Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs Only) and the 
interest accrued shall be deposited in the account of 
the respondent no.2.  The bank account details of the 
son as well as the respondent no.2 shall be provided 
by the learned counsel for the respondent no.2 in the 
registry within seven days from today whereupon, the 
registry shall transfer the amounts as indicated 
above in the respective bank accounts.  
13. Learned Counsel for the appellant , on 
instructions, has stated that the appellant who is 
settled in Dubai shall not claim any visitation right in 
respect of his son, who has been under the care and 
protection of the respondent no.2  for more than 
twelve years.   
14. We have taken note of the settlement arrived at 
between the parties. The dispute between the parties 
arises from matrimonial discord.  The parents of the 
appellant stand acquitted, the marriage between the 
parties has been dissolved, and during the pendency 
of proceedings in this Court, the parties have resolved 
their differences on the terms recorded above. Under 
these circumstances, we are of the considered view 
that the continuation of the criminal proceedings 
arising out of FIR No.66 dated 7th July, 2012 would 

--- Page 211 ---
7 
 
serve no useful purpose. Although the challenge 
before the High Court was confined to the order dated 
11th October, 2013, declaring the appellant to be a 
proclaimed offender, we consider it appropriate, in 
the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case and 
in order to bring the litigation between the parties to 
an end, to exercise the powers vested in this Court 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. 
15. Accordingly, FIR No.66 dated 7th July, 2012 
registered at Police Station Nangal, District 
Rupnagar, Punjab, and all proceedings emanating 
therefrom, including the proclamation proceedings 
and the order dated 11th October, 2013 declaring the 
appellant a proclaimed offender, along with all 
consequential processes, stand quashed. 
16. It is specifically provided that, in terms of the 
statement made on his behalf, the appellant shall not 
be entitled to claim either custody rights or visitation 
rights in respect of the son. 
17. The impugned order is set aside, and the appeal 
is allowed accordingly.  
 

--- Page 212 ---
8 
 
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION 
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025 
PRIYANKA RAVINDRA UNIYAL        …PETITIONER 
VERSUS  
DHIRAJ PRASAD  
JAYANTIPRASAD NAUTIYAL            …RESPONDENT 
 
O R D E R 
1. The present transfer petition has been filed by the petitioner-
wife under Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, 
seeking transfer of Petition No. 38 of 2025, instituted by the 
respondent-husband under Sections 13(1)(ia) and 13(1)(ib) of 
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, seeking dissolution of 
marriage, from the Family Court, Thane, Maharashtra, to the 
Family Court, Dehradun, Uttarakhand. 
2. The marriage between the parties was solemnized on 28 th 
November, 2017, according to Hindu rites and customs. No 
child was born out of the wedlock. 
3. The parties have been residing separately since April, 2021. 
4. In 2025, the respondent -husband instituted Petition No. 38 
of 2025 before the Family Court, Thane, Maharashtra, 
seeking dissolution of marriage on the grounds of cruelty and 
desertion, alleging that the petitioner -wife had deserted him 
since 27th April, 2021. 

--- Page 222 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  2 
 
5. It is the aforesaid proceeding which the petitioner-wife seeks 
to have transferred, resulting in the filing of the present 
transfer petition. 
6. This Court, vide order dated 9 th April, 2026, referred the 
disputes between the parties to mediation. Pursuant thereto, 
the parties entered into a Settlement Agreement dated 16 th 
July, 2026, amicably resolving their matrimonial disputes. 
7. We have perused the Settlement Agreement. The parties have 
affirmed that the settlement has been arrived at voluntarily, 
of their own free will and without any coercion, duress, undue 
influence, fraud or collusion. They have further affirmed that 
all disputes and differences arising out of their matrimonial 
relationship have been amicably resolved, that no claims or 
demands remain outstanding against each other, and that 
there is no possibility of reconciliation between them. 
8. The material terms of the Settlement Agreement are 
reproduced hereinbelow: - 
“4. The parties entered into a settlement on 16.07.2026 
the following terms & conditions.: 
 
I. That First Party and Second Party (Petitioner and 
Respondent) hereto confirm and declare that they 
have voluntarily and of their own free will have 
decided not to live together as husband and wife 
and have arrived at this Settlement in the presence 
of the Mediator, the Counsel for the Petitioner wife, 
Counsel for Respondent husband. 
 
II. That parties have one case pending against each 
other as follows:- 
a) Respondent/ Husband has filed Divorce 
Petition No. 38 of 2025, titled as Mr. Dhiraj 

--- Page 223 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  3 
 
Prasad Jayantiprasad Nautiyal Vs Priyanka 
Ravindra Uniyal pending before Ld. Principal 
Judge Family Court, Thane. 
 
III. The Respondent husband has agreed to pay Rs. 
17,00,000 (Rupees Seventeen Lakhs Only) to the 
Petitioner wife towards full and final settlement of 
all her claims towards alimony, maintenance 
(past, present and future), Stridhan , belongings 
and any other claim whatsoever. In view of the 
terms of this settlement -agreement, both the 
parties herein undertake to withdraw / not press 
all other pending petitions/ cases filed by them (if 
any) against each and each other’s family 
members before any court of law or any other 
forum and would take all necessary steps for the 
same. The said sum of Rs. 17,00,000 (Rupees 
Seventeen Lakhs Only) via RTGS/ NEFT/ Demand 
Draft / Online Mode in the account bearing No. 
31240454450, IFSC Code. SBIN00006 84, Branch 
State Bank of India Mussoorie of Petitioner/wife 
shall be paid to the Petitioner as agreed by the 
parties is mentioned herein under:- 
 
a) The Respondent-husband shall pay an amount 
of Rs.5,00,000/ - (Five Lakh Only) by way of 
transfer/Demand Draft payable at Mussoorie in 
the name of (Priyanka Ravindra Uniyal) on the 
date of signing the settlement. 
 
b) Balance amount of Rs 5,00,000(Five Lakhs) 
shall by way of transfer/Demand Draft payable 
at Mussoorie in the name of (Priyanka Ravindra 
Uniyal) on date of filing of joint petition within 7 
days of signing the settlement. 
 
c) Balance amount of Rs 7,00,000(Seven Lakhs) 
shall by way of transfer/Demand Draft payable 
at Mussoorie in the name of (Priyanka Ravindra 
Uniyal) on date of final order by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court before the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court of India. 

--- Page 224 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  4 
 
IV. Parties confirm and declare that they shall jointly 
pray before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India for 
disposing of the present the Transfer Petition  
(Civil) No.3066/2025 and grant a decree of divorce 
by mutual consent by exercising its inherent 
power under Article 142 of the Constitution of 
India in the interest of parties who have been living 
apart for long and granting a decree of divorce 
straightaway shall enable the unwilling parties to 
end their untold misery. Parties agree to move a 
joint application before the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
requesting to quash / close the aforesaid pending 
proceeding and granting the decree of divorce by 
mutual consent. 
 
V. Alternatively, Parties have further agreed that in 
case for any reason, the Hon’ble Supreme Court is 
not inclined to invoke Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India for granting the decree of 
divorce by mutual consent or for quashing the 
above-mentioned ca se filed by the Respondent 
against the Petitioner, they shall take following 
steps to give effect to this present Settlement 
Agreement: - 
 
i. Parties shall, within 15 days from the date 
of the final order of the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court of India disposing of the present 
Transfer Petition (C) No. 3066 of 2025 
initiate proceedings to withdraw all 
litigations/ complaints/ cases (if any) filed 
by them against each other and are pending 
in various courts/authorities. All these 
cases (if any) will be withdrawn before the 
Second Motion. 
 
ii. Parties thereafter shall file Petition for 
divorce by mutual consent under Section 
13(B) of Hindu Marriage Act, before the 
competent Court at Dehradoon, or the 
competent court as directed by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court. It is agreed between the 
parties that both the motions for divorce will 

--- Page 225 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  5 
 
be filed together along with the  waiver 
application. The expenses of filing  both the 
mutual consent divorce petitions  by way of 
First and Second Motion  respectively shall 
be borne by the respective parties. 
 
iii. The Second Party shall pay to First Party  
balance amount of Rs 7,00,000/ -only by 
way of Demand Draft in favour of Ms. 
Priyanka Ravindra Uniyal at the time of 
recording of  statements during Second 
Motion of divorce  petition filed under 
Section 13(B)(2) of H.M. Act, 1955 by way of 
mutual consent. 
 
VI. Parties have further agreed, resolved and  
unequivocally state that they shall not initiate any 
further civil/criminal complaint/case or other  
proceedings before any court/forum or authority  
against each other and/or their family members 
and in case any case/complaint/ proceedings are 
found to be pending before any 
court/forum/authority, the same shall be deemed 
to have been settled in terms  of the present 
Settlement Agreement. 
 
VII. Parties also agree and undertake not to  interfere 
in the life of each other in any manner  and also 
undertake not to make any allegations, defamatory 
or derogatory, against each other and  their 
respective family members personally or on  any 
public forum and/or through telephonic mode,  
social media i.e. whatsapp, facebook, twitter,  
instagram etc. or in any other manner 
whatsoever.” 
 
9. Accordingly in terms of Para IV and V of the Settlement 
Agreement dated 16th July, 2026, a joint application, I.A. No. 
229016 of 2026, has been  filed under Article 142 of the 
Constitution seeking divorce by mutual consent.  

--- Page 226 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  6 
 
10. We have considered the Settlement Agreement dated 16 th 
July, 2026, and the statements made by the parties before 
us. Having regard to the fact that the parties have been living 
separately for more than five years, that all disputes arising 
out of their matrimonial relationship have been amicably 
resolved, that the settlement has been arrived at voluntarily 
and without coercion, and that there is no possibility of 
reconciliation between them, we are satisfied  that the 
settlement is genuine, voluntary and bona fide and deserves 
to be given effect to. 
11. Admittedly, the respondent -husband has paid Rs. 
10,00,000/- out of the total agreed sum of Rs. 17,00,000/ -. 
The balance amount of Rs. 7,00,000/ - the parties had 
mutually agreed shall be paid on the date of final order 
passed by this Court. It has been fairly submitted at bar that 
the remaining balance amount of Rs. 7,00,000/ - has also 
been paid by the respondent-husband on 20th August, 2026. 
12. We place on record our appreciation for the commendable 
efforts of Mr. Sampa Sengupta Ray, learned Mediator at the 
Supreme Court Mediation Centre, whose sincere and effective 
efforts facilitated the amicable resolution of the disputes 
between the parties. 
13. In view of the aforesaid circumstances, we are of the 
considered view that the present case is a fit case for exercise 
of the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 142 of the 
Constitution of India so as to bring a quietus to the disputes 
between the parties and secure complete justice. 

--- Page 227 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  7 
 
14. Accordingly, I.A. No. 229016 of 2026 is allowed in terms of 
the Settlement Agreement dated 16 th July, 2026. In exercise 
of our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, 
we issue the following directions: - 
i. In lieu of relegating the parties to approach the 
competent Family Court by filing a petition  for divorce 
by mutual consent  under Section 13 -B of the Hindu 
Marriage Act, 1955, this Court has exercised its powers 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.  
ii. The marriage solemnized between the petitioner -wife 
and the respondent-husband on 28th November, 2017 
is hereby dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual 
consent. 
iii. Accordingly, HMA Petition No. 38 of 2025, titled “Dhiraj 
Prasad Jayantiprasad Nautiyal v. Priyanka Ravindra 
Uniyal”, pending before the learned Family Court, 
Thane, Maharashtra, shall stand disposed of. 
iv. Any other case, complaint, proceeding, petition, suit or 
litigation, whether civil or criminal, pending between the 
parties and arising out of or in connection with their 
matrimonial relationship or the disputes and differences 
settled under the Settlement Agreement dated 16th July, 
2026, shall also stand quashed, withdrawn and/or 
closed, as the case may be. 
v. As a necessary measure, the parties shall not hereafter 
initiate, institute or pursue any fresh complaint, 
proceeding, petition, suit or other litigation against each 

--- Page 228 ---
T.P. (CIVIL) NO. 3066 OF 2025  8 
 
other or their respective family members arising out of 
or in connection with their marriage or the matrimonial 
disputes and differences which have been settled 
between them. 
15. The Registry is further directed, in terms of paragraph (d) of 
the prayer clause of I.A. No. 229016 of 2026, to correct the 
name of the respondent -husband from “ Dhiraj Prasad 
Jayantiprasand Nautiyal ” to “ Dhiraj Prasad Jayantiprasad 
Nautiyal” in both the transfer petition and the Settlement 
Agreement dated 16th July, 2026. 
16. Consequently, the present transfer petition stands disposed 
of.  
17. The Registry shall draw up the decree of divorce accordingly, 
after carrying out the aforesaid correction in the name of the 
respondent-husband, in terms of paragraph 15 of this order. 
18. Pending application(s), if any, are disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO.  1878/2025
WITH
I.A. NO.283204/2026
 IN
 TRANSFER PETITION (C) NO.   2226/2019  
TAVINDER KAUR @ SACHI                           PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
HARINDER SINGH                                  RESPONDENT(S)
 
O R D E R
The Transfer Petition was filed by the petitioner-wife in
which she sought the following prayers:
“(a) Transfer  the  Divorce  Petition  No.3308  of  2019
(461/2019) titled as ‘Dr. Harinder Singh vs. Dr.
Tavinder Kaur @ Sachi’ pending before Court of
Family Court No.1 Jaipur Rajasthan to competent
Family Court Jharsuguda Orissa; and/or
(b) Pass such other order/orders as this Hon’ble Court
may  deem  fit  and  proper  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case.”
This Court vide order dated 28.07.2022 had allowed the
Transfer Petition with direction that the said divorce case be
decided within a period of six months. 
Consequently, during the pendency of the said Divorce
Petition, renumbered as C.P. Case No.91/2022 before the Family
Court,  Jharsuguda  (Orissa),  the  present  Miscellaneous
Application  has  been  filed  before  this  Court  by  the
applicant/respondent-husband sought the following prayers:

--- Page 238 ---
2
“(a) Pass appropriate directions inter alia fixing fresh
time frame as per order dated 28.07.2022 passed in
T.P. (C)  No.2226 of 2019; and
(b) Pass such other order or orders as this Hon’ble
Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the present case.”
During the pendency of this Miscellaneous Application,
in order to explore the possibility of a settlement between the
parties,  the  parties  were  referred  to  the  Supreme  Court
Mediation Centre.
Learned counsel for the respective parties submits that
the parties have arrived at a mediated settlement and a copy of
the Settlement Agreement dated 09.05.2026 has been filed. 
Learned counsel for the respective parties also submitted
that the parties have decided to part ways and the parties have
filed a joint application being  I.A. NO.283204/2026  under
Article  142  of  the  Constitution  of  India  for  seeking
dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce by mutual
consent.  Learned  counsel  for  the  respective  parties  have
submitted that on 09.06.2026, the parties have arrived at a
settlement and a Settlement Agreement has been drawn up, signed
by both the parties before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre. 
Learned counsel for the respective parties also submitted
that a sum of Rs.1,38,00,000/-(Rupees One Crore and Thirty
Eight Lakhs only) by RTGS/Demand Draft in the name of Dr.
Tavinder  Kaur  @  Sachi  in  Account  No.50100091134772,  IFSC
No.HDFC0000763, HDFC bank, Branch Jharsuguda, Orissa has been
paid by the respondent-husband to the petitioner-wife towards

--- Page 239 ---
3
full and final settlement of all her claims and the receipt of
the  said  amount  is  acknowledged  by  the  petitioner-wife.
Further, 250 grams (Two Hundred and Fifty Grams) 24 carat gold
in the form of physical MMTC Gold coin has been handed over to
the petitioner-wife herein. 
Learned counsel for the respective parties, therefore,
submitted that the Settlement Agreement may be taken on record.
The parties have also filed a joint application under Article
142 of the Constitution of India seeking a decree of divorce by
mutual consent. The same has also been signed by both the
parties and hence, both the learned counsel for the parties
prayed that this Court may take on record the said application
and dissolve the marriage between the parties by a decree of
divorce by mutual consent.
The parties are present before this Court. They have been
identified by their respective counsel. When queried by this
Court, they stated that they have indeed agreed to part ways on
certain terms and conditions which have been delineated in the
Settlement Agreement and that the settlement terms as well as
the joint application filed by them may be taken on record and
the matter may be, accordingly, disposed of. 
They  further  stated  that  they  have  arrived  at  a
settlement on their own free will without there being any
coercion or undue influence from any side. It is also stated by
both the parties that they would comply with the terms and
conditions of the Settlement Agreement. 

--- Page 240 ---
4
In the above backdrop, the Settlement Agreement as well
as the application filed under Article 142 of the Constitution
of India are taken on record and perused. 
It is also noted that the following cases have been filed
by the parties against each other:
“(i) CP No.91 of 2022 pending before the Ld. Family
Court, Jharsuguda, Orissa filed by the Respondent-
husband.
(ii) CMC No.315 of 2023 a complaint case filed under
Section 12 of DV Act by Dr. Tavinder Kaur against
Dr. Harinder Singh and his family pending in the
Court of Senior Civil Judge, Jharsuguda (Women’s
Court) (previously as CMC No.118 of 2019 in the
Court of SDJM, Jharsuguda.
(iii) Criminal Case being CT 242 of 2022 pending Ld.
Court of J.M.F.C. Jharsuguda, Orissa which arose
out of FIR No,187 of 2019 under Sections 498-A, 34
of IPC r/2 Section 4 of D.P. Act registered on
complaint of Dr. Tavinder Kaur at P.S. Brajraj
Nagar, Jharsuguda, Orissa.
(iv) Criminal complaint No.113 of 2019 filed before the
Court of ACMM, Jaipur for offence under Section
420, 406, 506, 509 r/2 120 B of IPC against the
petitioner and her family members.
(v) FIR  No.0663  of  2019  dated  29.11.2019  at  P.S.
Jaipur, against the Petitioner for offence under
Section 66(1), 66(E), 67A of IT Act.
(VI) Civil Suit No.414 of 2023 filed at the Court of Ld.
ADJ, Jaipur, Metro HQ-II against the Petitioner’s
father & others-the same is pending at the stage of
framing of issues.
(VII) Writ Petition (Civil) No. 1282 of 2025 pending
before the Hon’ble High Court of Orissa at Cuttack
filed by the Petitioner-wife.
(VIII) C.R.L. MC No.4725 of 2024 pending before the
Hon’ble High Court of Orissa at Cuttack filed by
the Respondent-husband.

--- Page 241 ---
5
(IX) Criminal Misc. Case No.81 of 2024 pending before
Ld. ADJ, Jaipur, Rajasthan filed by the father of
the  Respondent-Husband  against  father  of
petitioner-wife.
(X) Any  other  pending  cases/complaints  (Civil  or
Criminal) against either parties and their family
members or friends, if any.”
The above mentioned cases filed by the parties against
each other are quashed.  
We have perused the terms of settlement agreed to by the
parties as well as the joint application ( I.A. NO.283204/2026)
filed under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. We find
that the said terms are lawful and there is no legal impediment
in accepting the same. 
In the circumstances, we accept the settlement terms.
Hence,  I.A. NO.283204/2026  filed under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India seeking divorce, is allowed.
Consequently, the marriage between the parties which was
solemnized on 29.03.2015 at Raipur, Chhattisgarh is dissolved
by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 
The terms of settlement shall be read as part and parcel
of this order. 
The Registry to draw-up a decree accordingly.

The Miscellaneous Application is disposed of in the
aforesaid terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          Upon hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Ms. Archana Pathak Dave, learned Additional Solicitor
General submitted that pursuant to the judgment dated 04 th
August, 2026, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and
Climate Change (MoEF&CC) has filed an affidavit, which is
to the following effect:
“1. That, I am well acquainted with the facts and
circumstances  of  the  present  case  and  duly
authorized to sign the present affidavit
2. That the present affidavit is being filed in
compliance  to  the  order  dated  04.08.2026,
whereby, inter alia, MoEF&CC has been directed to
take into account the principles referred to in
the said order for determination and imposition
of environmental compensation, as also the Rules
that  operate  in  the  field,  to  formulate  the
necessary guidelines  to be  issued under  Rule
17(2) of the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026
(hereinafter referred to as "SWM Rules, 2026"),
and place on record the progress in the making
and the issuance of regulations.
3. It is humbly submitted that, as per sub-rule
(2) of Rule 17 of the SWM Rules, 2026, the
Central  Implementation  Committee  (hereinafter
referred to  as 'CIC")  constituted by  Central
Pollution Control Board (CPCB) under these rules
shall  prepare  guidelines  for  imposition  and
collection  of  environment  compensation  from
entities  involved  in  collection,  sorting,
transportation and treatment or processing of
solid waste and disposal, in case of violation or
non- compliance under the rules. That the Central
Implementation  Committee  (CIC)  has  been
constituted by the CPCB  vide Office Memorandum
dated 09.03.2026, and is chaired by the Chairman,
CPCB.
3

--- Page 283 ---
4. It is humbly submitted that in compliance with
the directions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court dated
04.08.2026, MoEF&CC forwarded the judgment/order
of this Hon'ble Court, vide Office Memorandum
dated  25.08.2026,  to  the  Central  Pollution
Control Board (hereinafter referred to as 'CPCB')
for taking necessary action and for placing the
matter before the CIC for preparation of the
necessary Environmental Compensation guidelines
under Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026. Copy of
the Office Memorandum dated 25.08.2026 is annexed
and marked as Annexure-I.
5. It is humbly submitted that, pursuant thereto,
the second meeting of the Central Implementation
Committee  (CIC)  was  convened  on  25.09.2026
through hybrid mode under the chairmanship of the
Chairman, Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
The meeting was attended by the Members of the
Committee  and  officials  of  the  Regional
Directorates of the CPCB and its Head Office,
Delhi.
6.  It  is  humbly  submitted  that,  during  the
meeting, the Members were, inter alia, apprised
of  the  order  dated  04.08.2026  passed  by  the
Hon'ble Supreme Court regarding the formulation
of Guidelines under Rule 17(2) of the Solid Waste
Management Rules, 2026 for the determination and
imposition of Environmental Compensation. After
detailed deliberations, the following decisions
were taken with respect to the formulation of the
said Guidelines:
(1)  A  Sub-Committee  comprising
representatives from the selected Expert
Institution(s)/Technical  Agency(ies)  and
CIC may be constituted for preparation of
"Guidelines for imposition and collection
of EC", under SWM Rules, 2026.
(2) The Draft Guidelines may be placed for
consideration  of  the  CIC  in  its  next
meeting, scheduled to be held within one
month.
Copy of the minutes of meeting dated 26.09.2026
is annexed and marked as Annexure-II.
7. That, in view of the facts and circumstances
stated  hereinabove,  it  is  most  respectfully

1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur, by
the impugned judgment and order dated 17 th June,
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.13748/2026  1

--- Page 293 ---
2026, has rejected the appellant’s second application
for bail in anticipation of arrest. 
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No.0002
of 2026 dated 22 nd January, 2026 registered at Police
Station  Borai,  District  Dhamtari  under  Sections
318(4),  338,  339  and  340  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita (BNS), 2023 and 19(4) of the Chhattisgarh
Krishi Upaj Mandi Adhiniyam, 1972 (Mandi Act).

5. The counter affidavit records that the appellant
has been cooperating with the Investigating Officer.
6. In view thereof, we are of the considered opinion
that the  appellant’s  detention  for  custodial
interrogation is not necessary and that he may be
admitted to an order for grant of bail in anticipation
of arrest.
7. We,  accordingly,  set  aside  the  judgment  and
order impugned in this appeal.
8. It is directed that in the event of the appellant

being arrested, he shall be released on bail on terms
and conditions to be imposed by the trial court.
9. Since  the  investigation  is  yet  to  conclude,  we
direct that if the investigating officer calls upon the
appellant  to  continue  to  join  the  investigation,  he
shall  do  so  by  attending  the  police  station  failing
which liberty is granted to bring any such omission to
the notice of the trial court and seek cancellation of
bail.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the
facts of the case from disclosing such facts to any
police officer or to the court.
11. We  clarify  that  the  observations  made  in  this
order and grant of bail to the appellant in anticipation
of arrest will not be treated as findings on the merits
of the case.
12. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the
aforesaid terms.

1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur,
by the impugned judgment and order dated 23 rd July, 2026,
has rejected the appellants’ application for grant of bail.
3. Appellants, figuring as accused in FIR No.0159 of 2026
dated 06th June, 2026 registered at Police Station Rishabhdev,
District Udaipur, Rajasthan  under Sections 299, 302 and
196(1)(a) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023 and
Sections 3 and 5(1) of the Rajasthan Prohibition of Unlawful

--- Page 299 ---
2
Conversion of Religion Act, 2025, were arrested on 06th June,
2026.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the counter-affidavit of the respondent-State of
Rajasthan.
5. Charge-sheet has been filed on 01 st September, 2026.
Prosecution proposes to examine 30 witnesses to drive home
the charges against the appellants. 
6. It also appears that 14th October, 2026 is the date fixed
for hearing arguments on charges. Thus, trial will take some
time to conclude.
7. Taking an overall view of the matter, coupled with the
nature of allegations levelled and the likely time to be taken
to complete the trial, we are of the considered opinion that
further detention of the appellants is not necessary; and,
since the appeal deserve acceptance, the appellants may be
admitted to an order for grant of bail pending trial.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.

3

shall not, directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        /2026
(@ SLP(C) No. 14486/2025)
THE COMMISSIONER, MYSORE URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AUTHORITY 
APPELLANT(S)
       VERSUS
LT. GEN. (RETD.) BNBM PRASAD & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. Challenge in this appeal is to the judgment dated 29.01.2025
passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Writ
Petition No. 14296/2024 (GM-Con). 
3. The said writ petition was filed against the order passed by
the Karnataka State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission 1 on
11.01.2024, whereby the appeal filed by the appellant - Mysore
Urban Development Authority 2, was allowed and  the complaint
filed by respondent No. 1 was dismissed.
4. Though we find merit in the contention of the learned counsel
for the Authority that the High Court was not justified in
entertaining a writ petition against an order passed by the
1  ‘SCDRC’ for short
2  ‘Authority’ for short
1

--- Page 305 ---
SCDRC in exercise of appellate jurisdiction as an effective
alternative remedy, by way of a revision, was available to
respondent  No.  1  under  the  provisions  of  the  Consumer
Protection Act, 1986, we are of the opinion that, given the
facts and circumstances of the case, the interest of justice
requires us to exercise our jurisdiction under Article 142 of
the Constitution of India so as to  give a quietus to the
matter instead of driving the parties to another round of
litigation. 
5. It is an admitted fact that respondent No. 1 was allotted a
site by the Authority under ‘Ex-servicemen’ category as long
back as on 25.02.2001.  Respondent No. 1 paid a sum of
5,000/-(Rupees five thousand only) along with his application₹
and though there was some delay on his part in paying the
first installment of 24,000 (Rupees twenty four thousand) and₹
the balance amount of 1,31,000/- (Rupees one lakh thirty one₹
thousand), the irrefutable fact remains that those payments
were made with just a few months’ delay.  The sum of 24,000/-₹
(Rupees twenty four thousand), which was to be paid within 15
days of the issuance of the sanction letter dated 25.02.2001,
was paid on 02.06.2001, while the sum of 1,31,000/-(Rupees₹
one lakh thirty one thousand), which was to be paid within 90
days, was paid on 29.11.2001.
6. Having received the aforestated sums of money from respondent
No. 1, the Authority failed to take action, either for
execution of the lease deed in favour of respondent No. 1 or
2

--- Page 306 ---
to cancel the allotment in his favour. It is in this context
that  respondent  No.  1  approached  the  District  Consumer
Disputes Redressal Forum3, Mysore.
7. By order dated 22.07.2016, the DCDRF directed the Authority to
allot the site bearing No. 566 situated in Hanchya-Sathagally
B-Zone and execute necessary documents for handing over the
possession of the same to respondent No. 1 within a time
frame. In the event of default, the Authority was to pay
penalty of 500/- (Rupees five hundred only) per day to₹
respondent  No.  1.  In  addition  thereto,  compensation  of
10,000/-(Rupees ten thousand) towards deficiency in service₹
and costs of 2000/- (Rupees two thousand) were also to be₹
paid within a time frame, failing which they were to carry
interest at the rate of 10% per annum.
8. Aggrieved by the said order, the Authority approached the
SCDRC, by way of an appeal, which was allowed on 11.01.2024
resulting in the dismissal of the consumer complaint itself.
The said order was subjected to challenge before the High
Court by way of Writ Petition No. 14296/2024 (GM-Con) by
respondent No. 1.
9. By the impugned order, a Division Bench of the High Court
allowed the writ petition, quashing the order passed by the
SCDRC and restoring the order of the DCDRF. 
10. However,  while  confirming  the  payments  to  be  made  to
respondent No. 1, in terms of the order passed by the DCDRF,
3  “DCDRF”, for short
3

--- Page 307 ---
the Division Bench permitted the Authority to deduct 21,930/-₹
(Rupees twenty one thousand nine hundred thirty), claimed by
it as interest on delayed payments. 
11. Given the fact that respondent No. 1 paid the full amount for
allotment of the site in the year 2001 itself, with a just few
months’ delay, and the fact that he was not allotted the site
till date, despite the Authority not resorting to cancellation
of the allotment, it is not open to the Authority to assert
that it is not liable to make good on the allotment or
compensate respondent No. 1 for retaining his monies while
denying him the possession and enjoyment of the site. 
12. Upon instructions, the learned counsel appearing for the
Authority, informed this Court that the site bearing No. 566
is still available for allotment to respondent No. 1. 
13. In that view of the matter, this appeal is disposed of,
directing the Authority to allot the site in question to
respondent  No.  1;  execute  all  necessary  documents  in
connection therewith; and deliver possession thereof to him
within 30 days from today. 
14. Further,  as  the  Authority  retained  the  monies  paid  by
respondent No. 1 for all these years though he got no benefit
out of the same and as he was also driven to litigation
stretching over more than a decade, we deem it appropriate to
direct  the  Authority  to  pay  compensation  of  2,40,000/-₹
(Rupees two lakhs forty thousand only) to respondent No. 1.
This compensation shall also be paid within the aforestated
4

--- Page 308 ---
time frame of 30 days from today. 
15. The orders passed by the DCDRF and the High Court shall stand
set aside to the extent they direct otherwise.
     Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
..........................J.
(SANJAY KUMAR)
..........................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)
NEW DELHI;
SEPTEMBER 29, 2026.

O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. On 29.03.2025, police at Mauganj Police Station
intercepted  an  unregistered  Toyota  Glanza  Car  and
recovered 2160 bottles of Onrex cough syrup which
1

--- Page 311 ---
contained codeine phosphate from the occupants of the
vehicle, namely, Amit Singh, Ashish Patel and Amol Tiwari.
Hence, an FIR came to be registered for the offences
punishable under Sections 8A(c),  21 and 22 of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
(“NDPS Act”) and Sections 5 and 13 of the M.P. Drugs
Control Act. During the course of the investigation, the co-
accused disclosed the involvement of Rahul Dwivedi (@
SLP (CRL.) NO.9072/2026 ) as the procurer of the syrup,
Sumit Keshari @ Amit as the illegal supplier through his

4. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the

Singh) is said to have rented out his vehicle. Undisputedly,

by him is an issue which will have to be examined after
trial. Hence, we are of the view that the appellant –
2

--- Page 312 ---
Anirudh  Singh  would  be  entitled  for  grant  of  bail.

is set aside and appellant is ordered to be released on bail

may deem fit to impose.
5. Insofar as the prayer of the appellant – Rahul
Dwivedi (@ SLP (CRL.) NO.9072/2026 ) is concerned, we

sought for him. The other material that has been collected
during the course of investigation requires to be evaluated
by the trial court. That apart, there are two witnesses who
are  to  be  examined.  Taking  into  consideration,  the
antecedent of the appellant – Rahul Dwivedi (@ SLP (CRL.)
NO.9072/2026),  who  is  having  more  than  eight
antecedents and three cases relate to NDPS Act, we are of
the  considered  view  the  he  is  not  entitled  for the
discretionary relief at this stage. Hence, we reserve liberty
to him for reviving his prayer after conclusion of the trial
3

--- Page 313 ---

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION (C) NO(S).60/2026
11.1 KM-S PTE- LTD. PETITIONER(S)
                              VERSUS
UPGRAD EDUCATION PVT. LTD. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The instant petition has been filed under section
11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996
Act) seeking appointment of a Sole Arbitrator for the
adjudication of disputes that have arisen between the
parties.
2. The  Petitioner is  a body  corporate incorporated
under the laws of Singapore, and is engaged in providing
consultancy and advisory services, while the Respondent is
an Indian company engaged in online higher education and
professional upskilling services. 
3. A Consultancy Agreement dated 30.12.2021 (Agreement)
was  executed  between  the  Petitioner  and  Talentedge
Education Ventures Private Limited (Talentedge), under
which the Petitioner agreed to render consultancy services
to facilitate partnerships with Indian universities. In
April 2022, the Respondent acquired Talentedge. Following
the same, the Petitioner and the Respondent executed
1

--- Page 317 ---
Addendum-I dated 28.03.2023. Significantly, in its reply
dated 21.11.2025, the Respondent itself described the
Consultancy Agreement read with Addendum-I as an agreement
executed between the Respondent and the Petitioner and
expressed  its  willingness  to  refer  the  disputes  to
arbitration under Clause 11.2.
4. As per Clause 11.2 of the Agreement, all disputes
arising out of or in connection with the Agreement shall
be    resolved by binding arbitration under the 1996 Act,
the arbitrator being selected by mutual agreement of the
parties or, failing agreement within thirty days of a
written notice, in accordance with the provisions of the
1996  Act.  Additionally,  the  seat  and  venue  of  the
arbitration would be Mumbai, India.
5. It is the Petitioner’s case that the Respondent
stopped paying the royalty/consultancy fee from January
2025  and  failed  to  share  the  monthly  Management
Information System reports from February 2025 onwards.
Accordingly, the Petitioner sought to invoke arbitration
as contemplated in Clause 11.2 by issuing a notice dated
16.10.2025, in which it proposed the name of a Senior
Advocate to be appointed as the Sole Arbitrator. The
Respondent, by its reply dated 21.11.2025, rejected the
said proposal and, instead, proposed the name of an
Advocate, while also suggesting recourse to mediation. Be
that as it may, ultimately, the parties could not form
2

--- Page 318 ---
consensus  within  the  thirty-day  period  stipulated  in
Clause 11.2.
6. The  Petitioner  thereafter  filed  Commercial
Arbitration Application (L) No. 5484/2026 before the High
Court of Judicature at Bombay, which was withdrawn on
10.04.2026 with liberty to approach the appropriate forum.
Subsequently, the parties mutually agreed to appoint the
Advocate who was earlier proposed by the Respondent, as
the Sole Arbitrator. However, the Disclosure Statement
dated 11.05.2026, under Section 12(1) of the 1996 Act,
furnished by the said Advocate brought to light certain
conflicts, resulting in the Respondent’s objection to the
said appointment vide letter dated 15.05.2026. This series
of events resulted in the recusal of the Advocate from the
arbitral process on 18.05.2026.
7. On  18.06.2026,  the  Petitioner  proposed  another
Advocate  as  the  Sole  Arbitrator.  However,  the  same
proposal was not amenable to the Respondent, who declined
it  on  24.06.2026,  while  counter-proposing  two  other
Advocates’  names.  The  parties’  further  attempts  to
mutually appoint an arbitrator also regrettably failed. It
is in this factual backdrop that the Petitioner has
approached this Court.
8. We have heard learned Counsel for the parties and
perused the material placed on record.
3

--- Page 319 ---
9. Since  the  Petitioner  is  a  body  corporate
incorporated under the laws of Singapore, the proposed
arbitration is an international commercial arbitration
within the meaning of Section 2(1)(f)(ii) of the 1996 Act.
This Court consequently has jurisdiction under Section
11(6) read with Section 11(12)(a).
10. In  view  of  the  existence  of  the  arbitration
agreement, the invocation thereof, and the failure of the
parties to agree upon a sole arbitrator, the petition is
allowed. We appoint Justice Gautam S. Patel, former Judge
of the Bombay High Court as the Sole Arbitrator to
adjudicate the disputes between the parties arising out of
or in connection with the Consultancy Agreement dated
30.12.2021 read with Addendum-I dated 28.03.2023. The seat
and venue of the arbitration, in accordance with the said
agreement, shall be Mumbai, India.
11. The learned Arbitrator shall determine the fees and
other modalities of the arbitration in consultation with
the parties. The appointment shall be subject to the
learned Arbitrator furnishing the disclosure contemplated
by Section 12(1) read with the Sixth Schedule of the 1996
Act  and  there  being  no  legal  impediment  to  the
appointment.
12. All rights and contentions of the parties on the
merits, including their respective claims, counterclaims
4

--- Page 320 ---
and defences, are left open for determination by the
learned Arbitrator.
13. The Arbitration Petition is disposed of in the above
terms. Pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026  
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No(s).20008-20010 of 2026) 
 
GEETA BAI & ORS.                    ….APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
K. ARJUN SINGH & ORS.  ….RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R  
1. Heard. 
2. Leave granted.  
3. The appellants herein are aggrieved by the 
judgment and final order dated 28 th May, 2025 
passed by the High Court for the State of Telangana 
at Hyderabad 1 whereby Interlocutory Application 
Nos.1/2022, 3/2022 and 4/2022 filed by the 
appellants in Appeal Suit No.552 of 2009 were 
rejected on the ground of maintainability.  
4. The appellants herein had preferred three 
Interlocutory Applications before the High Court with 
the following prayers: IA No.1/2022, for recall of the 
compromise decree dated 23 rd September, 2020; IA 
 
1 Hereinafter, referred to as the “High Court”. 

--- Page 323 ---
2 
 
No.3/2022, seeking impleadment in O.S. No.473 of 
2000 as proper and necessary parties;  and IA 
No.4/2022, seeking to restrain the parties  to the 
proceedings from alienating or creating third party 
rights over the subject property in Appeal Suit  
No.552 of 2009.  
5. The appellants herein are the legal heirs of Late 
Smt. Ballo Bai, who was the daughter and legal heir 
of Late Shri Tikaram Singh. It is the specific case of 
the appellants that Smt. Ballo Bai was entitled to an 
undivided 1/4th share in the suit property by virtue 
of Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as 
amended by Act 39 of 2005. Original Suit for partition 
No.473 of 2000 was filed by Late  Shri Dhan Singh, 
son of Late  Shri Tikaram Singh, in the Court of IV  
Additional Senior Civil Judge  (FTC), Ranga Reddy 
District at L.B. Nagar against his brother Late Shri 
Satyanarayan Singh (defendant No.1), and the legal 
heirs of Late Shri Sheetal Singh, who was also a son 
of Late Shri Tikaram Singh and the brother of the 
plaintiff. 
6. However, Late Smt. Ballo Bai was not impleaded 
as a defendant in the suit. The trial Court dismissed 
the suit filed by Late Shri Dhan Singh, by judgment 

--- Page 324 ---
3 
 
and decree dated 30 th June, 2009. Aggrieved, the 
legal heirs of Late Shri Dhan Singh filed Appeal Suit 
No.552 of 2009 , again without impleading the legal 
heirs of Late Smt. Ballo Bai , i.e., the appellants 
herein, as respondents (Smt. Ballo Bai expired in the 
intervening period).  
7. The appellants in the said appeal (the legal heirs 
of Late Shri Dhan Singh) and the respondents therein 
entered into a memorandum of compromise 
partitioning the suit schedule property proportionally 
amongst themselves. The said compromise was 
accepted and taken on record by the High Court  
leading to  the judgment and decree  dated 23 rd 
September, 2020.  
8. The appellants claim that during the lifetime of 
Late Smt. Ballo Bai , her brothers i.e., Late Shri 
Satyanarayan Singh, Late  Shri Sheetal Singh and 
Late Shri Dhan Singh had promised to give an equal 
share to Late Smt. Ballo Bai and her legal heirs.   
9. Yet, Late Smt. Ballo Bai, the only daughter and 
legal heir of Late Shri Tikaram Singh, who according 
to the appellants had a rightful 1/4th share in the suit 
schedule property as per Section 6 of the Hindu 

--- Page 325 ---
4 
 
Succession Act, 1956, as amended by Act 39 of 2005, 
was not impleaded as a defendant in the suit. 
10. When the appellants herein came to know of the 
compromise recorded  behind their back  vide 
judgment and decree  dated 23 rd September, 2020, 
they moved the aforesaid applications before the High 
Court, which came to be  dismissed with the 
observation that the appellants could not ask for 
recall of the post -decretal arrangement made by the 
parties to the appeal  and that the  remedy of the 
appellants (applicants before the High Court) would 
be to file a separate suit or an appeal to the higher 
court after seeking leave of the court.  
11. Having heard and considered the submissions 
advanced by learned counsel for the parties and after 
going through the impugned order , we are of the 
opinion that the view taken by the High Court is 
erroneous and unsustainable in the eyes of  law.  By 
virtue of Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, 
as amended by Act 39 of 2005, Late Smt. Ballo Bai, 
being the legal heir of Late  Shri Tikaram Singh, was 
entitled to stake a claim for 1/4th share in the suit 
schedule property and hence, was  undoubtedly a 
necessary party to the proceedings.   

--- Page 326 ---
5 
 
12. The compromise  decree obtained by the 
brothers/legal heirs being the plaintiffs and the 
defendants without impleading Late Smt. Ballo Bai or 
her legal heirs, despite her being a necessary party to 
the suit, was a nullity in the eyes of law.  
13. By no stretch of imagination could Late Smt. 
Ballo Bai and her legal heirs be treated as strangers 
to the lis and thus they could not be disentitled from 
challenging the compromise and to seek recall of a 
decree obtained behind their back by virtue of the bar 
contained under Order XXIII Rule 3A of the CPC.  
14. Accordingly, we find the impugned order, 
rejecting the three Interlocutory Applications referred 
to supra, to be unsustainable in the eyes of law, and 
the same is thus set aside.  
15. The matter is remitted to the High Court to 
reconsider the aforesaid applications afresh in light 
of the observations made hereinabove. The interim 
order granted by this Court on 27 th May, 2026 shall 
remain in force for two weeks  from the date of this 
order.  
16. We make it clear that the extension of the 
interim order by this Court shall not influence the 
High Court in taking an independent decision on the 

--- Page 327 ---
6 
 
request for stay after hearing learned counsel for the 
parties in accordance with law. 
17. The parties shall appear before the High Court 
on 5th October, 2026. 
18. The third parties who have filed 
impleadment/intervention applications before this 
Court are also given liberty to approach the High 
Court and appear on 5th October, 2026. 
19. The appeals are allowed in these terms.  
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of.
