          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. These applications arise out of a chequered history entailing
disputes  regarding  identification  of  genuine  members  of  the
respondent-Society, as well as their entitlements. A long sequence
of litigation culminated the judgment dated 22.09.2022 passed in
Civil Appeal No. 6849/2022, whereby, in exercise of its powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution, this Court directed the New
Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) to allot multi-
storeyed flats to 844 identified members of the respondent-Society.
Further,  the  case  of  133  more  persons,  who  were  subsequent
purchasers, was directed to be examined, and if found satisfactory,
similar benefits were to be extended to them.
2. Thereafter,  certain  persons  claiming  to  be  original
members/subsequent purchasers approached this Court in M.A. No.
1700 of 2023, seeking benefit under the judgment dated 22.09.2022.
By way of order dated 25.07.2023, this Court permitted impleadment
of the said applicants and disposed of the application with a
direction to the Additional Chief Executive Officer, NOIDA, to
verify the genuineness of their claims and, if found eligible, to
3

--- Page 331 ---
take appropriate action to include them in the list of eligible
allottees. This Court also directed verification of the Society’s
claim that the correct figures were 858 original allottees and 119
subsequent purchasers, and not 844 and 133 respectively, as was
recorded in the judgment dated 22.09.2022.
3. Subsequently, the M.A. No. 2485/2023 came to be filed by the
respondent-Society,  submitting  that  the  verification  exercise
directed through order dated 25.07.2023 had stalled, and NOIDA had
not completed the exercise of ascertaining the identity of correct
and genuine members within the timelines fixed. Subsequently,
various other persons, whose names were not included in the
original  list  of  members  referred  to  in  the  judgment  dated
22.09.2022, filed their respective M.A.s seeking benefits either as
original members or subsequent purchasers.
4. These M.A.s have been taken up for hearing, and this Court has
issued interim directions from time to time.  Vide order dated
04.12.2023, NOIDA was directed to file a compliance affidavit with
regard to our order dated 25.07.2023 and to accord personal hearing
to the office-bearers of the Society. Thereafter, vide order dated
11.03.2024, the number of original members was revised to 863,
while the 120 subsequent purchasers were identified. NOIDA was also
directed to justify its stand that subsequent purchasers are not
entitled to be included in the list of eligible allottees.
5. In compliance therewith, an affidavit dated 30.07.2024 has
been filed on behalf of NOIDA, pointing out that the allotment
letters issued to the original members/allottees contained an
express provision prohibiting transfer of the plot without prior
4

--- Page 332 ---
permission of NOIDA. Moreover, it is submitted that the original
allotments were cancelled on 05.05.1998 and the amounts paid by the
original allottees were refunded. The respondent-Society, however,
submits that prior permission was not obtained only due to NOIDA’s
inaction and refusal qua transfer form(s) submitted by the original
allottees/members, and the Authority cannot now rely on its own
conduct to deny the claims of the allottees/their successors. The
Society  also  contended  that  neither  were  the  refund  cheques
encashed nor were the amounts subsequently redeposited.
6. At this juncture, more than three years have elapsed since the
judgment dated 22.09.2022, but the exercise of finally ascertaining
the genuine members of the respondent-Society remains incomplete on
account of the continuing dispute between NOIDA and the Society as
to the correct number and identity of eligible members.
7. Having regard to the fact that this process has remained
inconclusive  despite  repeated  affidavits  and  directions  and
considering that a large number of the original allottee-members
have been awaiting the fruits of litigation for over three decades,
we are satisfied that an independent verification mechanism to
decide the competing claims and implement this Court’s earlier
directions is necessary.
8. We  accordingly  invoke  our  powers  under  Article  142  and
constitute  a  one-member  High-Powered  Independent  Committee
comprising  Justice  Sudhir  Kumar  Saxena,  former  Judge  of  the
Allahabad High Court, to identify the genuine members of the
respondent-Society and ascertain their claims and entitlement qua
the benefits granted by the judgment dated 22.09.2022.
5

--- Page 333 ---
9. The one-member Committee shall be at liberty to devise its own
procedure, including calling for such documents and hearing the
concerned members/claimants as it may consider necessary. NOIDA,
the  respondent-Society,  and  all  claimants  shall  extend  full
cooperation to the one-member Committee and will make all relevant
records available for its consideration. We expect that this
exercise would be completed within eight weeks, whereupon the
Committee shall submit its report to this Court.
10. NOIDA shall make available required secretarial assistance and
logistical arrangements as per the requirements of the Committee.
The honorarium payable to Justice Saxena for his time and efforts,
to be borne by NOIDA, shall be determined on the next date of
hearing.
11. List on 02.12.2026.

1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, by
the impugned judgment and order dated 14.07.2026 in
Criminal Misc. Bail Application No. 2072 of 2026,
has rejected the appellant’s prayer for bail.
3. Appellant is figuring as an accused in FIR
No. 359 of 2024, registered at Police Station
Brijmanganj, District Maharajganj, under Sections
109(1), 190, 118(1), 191(2), 191(3), 115(2), 352,
1313 of the BNS1. 
4. As per the prosecution case, the victims were
assaulted by the appellant along with co-accused
1. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

--- Page 345 ---
Rahul @ Ram Mohan, Suraj, Atul and Dhruv Prajapati.
A perusal of the FIR though reveals their names,
however, it does not attribute any specific overt
act to each of the individual accused persons.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant
has drawn the attention of this Court to the orders
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  at
Allahabad, whereby similarly situated co-accused
have already been enlarged on bail, viz., Suraj
Sahani vide order dated 07.05.2025, Atul vide order
dated  28.07.2025,  and  Rahul  vide  order  dated
07.10.2025. It is contended that since identical
allegations are levelled against all the accused
persons, the appellant is entitled to the benefit
of parity. 
6. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing
for the respondent-State has vehemently opposed the
prayer for bail, submitted that the petitioner
along with co-accused persons assaulted the injured
victims. 
7. Having heard the learned counsel for the
parties  and  upon  careful  consideration  of  the
entire material on record, and taking into account
the period of incarceration already undergone by

--- Page 346 ---
the appellant as well as the fact that three
similarly  placed  co-accused  have  already  been
granted bail, this Court is of the opinion that the
appellant has made out a case for grant of bail.
The application for bail deserves to be allowed and
is allowed accordingly.
8. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned
judgment and order of the High Court.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject
to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of
the trial court and subject to such other terms and
conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly  or  indirectly,  by  making  inducement,
threat or promise, dissuade any person acquainted
with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms
and conditions for grant of bail, the trial court
shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the
appellant.
12. It is also ordered that the appellant shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending

--- Page 347 ---
the proceedings without justifiable cause, that
could also be seen as breach of the conditions for
grant of bail and the trial court will be free to
pass appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this
order and grant of bail will not be treated as
findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the
aforesaid terms.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No. 4629  OF 2026
[  @   SLP (Crl.) No……./2026 @ SLP(C) D.No. 14130 OF 2026]
SISHPAL BANSILAL YADAV                       APPELLANT
                           VERSUS
STATE OF GUJARAT                            RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R 
1.   Leave granted.
2. By the impugned judgment and order dated 18 th February,
2026, the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad has rejected the
appellant’s prayer for bail in anticipation of arrest.  
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 11211050250440
dated 15 th July, 2025 registered with Police Station-Thangadh,
District-Surendranagar, Gujarat. It is alleged in the FIR that the
appellant has committed offences punishable under Sections 65(a),
65(e), 81, 83, 116-B, 98(2) of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 and
Sections 111(2)(b), 111(3), 111(4), 336(2), 336(3), 340(2) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita  (BNS), 2023.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant as
well as the respondent.
1

--- Page 350 ---
5. It is not in dispute that the appellant is not named in the FIR.
He has been implicated as his truck was found to be involved in the
alleged offence. However, it is his stand that he had parted
possession of the truck pursuant to an agreement with a third party
and he is not in any manner responsible. Nonetheless, he has joined
the investigation in terms of our earlier order dated 2nd April, 2026.
6. In such view of the matter, we are of the opinion that custodial
interrogation of the appellant is not necessary and that there is
sufficient ground for the appellant to be admitted to an order for
grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
7. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set
aside.
8. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
9. It is made clear that in the event the appellant breaches any of
the terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not, directly or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
11. Also, since the investigation is yet to conclude, we direct that if
2

--- Page 351 ---
the investigating officer calls upon the appellant to join the
investigation, he shall do so by attending the police station.
12. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant of
bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
13. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
14.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Leave granted.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties.
The limited issue in this appeal is qua the
condition imposed by the High Court. The High
Court,  while  granting  regular  bail  to  the
appellant  in  FIR  No.10/2025,  registered  with
Police Station-Crime Branch, District-Gwalior, for
offences punishable under Sections 319(2), 318(4),
308(2), 336(2), 337, 338, 336(3), 340(2) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66-D of
the Information Technology Act, 2000, imposed a
condition on the appellant to pay a sum of Rs.5

--- Page 360 ---
2
lakhs with one surety of the like amount to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court.  Though the order
was passed based on the statement made by the
learned counsel appearing for the appellant, the
fact remains that the appellant is unable to
comply with the same. The appellant has already
been under incarceration for one year and four
months.  We could also infer that, notwithstanding
the fact that the order was passed on 11.03.2026,
the appellant continues to be under incarceration
due to his inability to comply with the condition
imposed by the High Court.
Taking note of the above, we are inclined to
set aside the condition imposed.
Accordingly, the condition to pay a sum of
Rs.5 lakh stands set aside and the appellant shall
be released on bail, subject to the terms and
conditions to the satisfaction of the concerned
Trial Court, unless and until he is required in
any other case.
The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.

1. Heard.

4. Appellant  was  apprehended  near  his  house  on
20.05.2025 and no contraband was found on his personal
search. Two sacks weighing 27.894 Kgs of Ganja was
recovered from the pit situated in bhatha land adjoining
the appellant’s house. Hence, FIR No.308/2025 came to be
1

--- Page 365 ---
registered for the offence punishable under Section 20(b)
of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act,
1985 (“NDPS Act”).
5. It is the case of the prosecution that appellant in a
memorandum of statement has admitted that absconding
co-accused Rakesh Verma had delivered 50 Kgs of Ganja
to appellant for the purpose of keeping the same out of
which 27 packets (27 kgs) remained with him and for this
safekeeping, he was paid Rs.5,000/-.
6. Chargesheet having been filed on conclusion of
investigation, trial has commenced and 10 out of 19
witnesses  have  been  examined  and  four  witnesses
including the Panch witness have turned hostile. As to
whether Section 37 of the NDPS Act was attracted is an
issue which will have to be thrashed out after trial,
particularly, in the background of the contraband not
having been recovered personally from appellant. As to
whether the place from which it was seized was in
exclusive ownership and custody of appellant and he
being in conscious possession of the contraband is an
2

--- Page 366 ---
issue which will have to be examined after trial. Hence, at
this stage, we are of the considered view that appellant is
entitled for grant of bail. Hence, appeal is allowed.

released on bail on such terms and conditions as the
jurisdictional Sessions Court may deem fit to impose.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(C) No. 30412/2025)
M/S. SHIV TEXTILES ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ICONIC IP INTERESTS, LLC ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.  Leave granted.
2. M/s. Shiv Textiles, the appellant, is a sole proprietorship,
represented by its proprietrix, Varshaben Kantilal Talreja.
She obtained the registration of Trademark No. 4075126 for
‘Jolly Ranger Legwear’ in Class-25 in respect of ‘Jeans Pants’
on 27.07.2019. She claims to have used the trademark from
01.01.2019.  While  so,  Iconic  IP  Interests,  LLC,  the
respondent, which was incorporated at Delaware in the United
States of America, issued legal notices dated 28.04.2023,
09.06.2023 and 17.08.2023 calling upon the appellant to cease
and desist from using its trademark on the ground that it had
been using ‘Jolly Rancher’ globally since 2004 for a variety
of goods, including those in Class-25. The respondent claimed
that it had started using it for candy in the year 1996.  
3. Admittedly, the respondent applied for registration of the
trademark ‘Jolly Rancher’ in Class-25 only on 07.06.2023 with
C.A. @ SLP(C) No. 30412/2025      1

--- Page 380 ---
the  user  detail  stated  as  ‘proposed  to  be  used’.  This
trademark is stated to have been registered on 09.10.2023.
4. Aggrieved by the legal notices issued to it, the appellant
filed  Commercial  Trade  Mark  Suit  No.  1/2023  before  the
Commercial Court, Bhavnagar, Gujarat, against the respondent.
This suit was filed praying for a declaration and a permanent
and perpetual injunction from infringement of the registered
trademark.  
5. While so, the respondent filed an application therein under
Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 1,
seeking rejection of the plaint on grounds of non-disclosure
of a cause of action and non-joinder of all the necessary
parties. However, by order dated 22.11.2024, the trial Court
rejected the said application, noting that the suit could not
be summarily dismissed at that juncture as the grounds taken
by the respondent did not fall within the ambit of Order VII
Rule 11 of the CPC.
6. Aggrieved  thereby,  the  respondent  filed  R/Special  Civil
Application  No.  1543/2025  under  Article  227  of  the
Constitution of India before the High Court of Gujarat at
Ahmedabad.  By the impugned judgment dated 09.05.2025, a
Division Bench of the High Court allowed the petition and
rejected the appellant’s plaint on the ground that there was
no cause of action.  This judgment is subjected to challenge
before us presently.
1  “CPC”, for short
C.A. @ SLP(C) No. 30412/2025      2

--- Page 381 ---
7. Significant to note, the respondent thereafter filed Civil
Suit (Commercial) No. 870/2023 before the Delhi High Court
against the proprietrix of the appellant, by name, praying for
a permanent injunction restraining her from manufacturing,
offering  for  sale,  selling,  displaying,  advertising  and
marketing ready made clothing, viz. Jeans and Pants, under the
mark ‘Jolly Ranger’, which is identically/deceptively similar
to its mark ‘Jolly Rancher’.
8. Having heard the learned counsel for the appellant and the
learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent, we are at
a loss to understand as to how the respondent can prevent the
appellant from maintaining a suit against it by claiming there
was no cause of action, despite issuing three cease and desist
notices  to  it.  Issuance  of  such  notices,  by  itself,
constituted a cause of action for the appellant to have
initiated legal proceedings against the respondent. Further,
institution of a suit by the respondent against the appellant
on the very same issue, that is, with regard to the registered
trademark being used by the appellant, clearly demonstrates
that the appellant did have a cause of action for filing a
suit.  
9. The High Court was, therefore, not justified in drawing the
inference there that was no cause of action for the appellant
to have filed a suit at that point of time.  Necessary
weightage was not attached to the fact that it was the
respondent that had created the cause of action for the
C.A. @ SLP(C) No. 30412/2025      3

--- Page 382 ---
appellant by issuing multiple cease and desist notices.  The
impugned judgment is, accordingly, set aside and Commercial
Trade Mark Suit No. 1/2023 is restored to the file of the
Commercial  Court,  Bhavnagar,  Gujarat.  Proceedings  therein
shall resume and continue in accordance with law.
10. The appeal is allowed in the aforestated terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.       OF 2026
(@ SLP(CRL.) No.17422/2026)
  STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.                      APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
CHOTKAU ALIAS ALLAUDDIN                            RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. We have heard the learned senior counsel appearing for the
parties qua the issue pertaining to the direction given by the
High Court to the Central Bureau of Investigation (for short,
the CBI) to conduct an inquiry into the correctness of
allegations levelled in F.I.R. No. 113 of 2025 lodged in
Police Station – Ikauna, District – Shravasti for the offences
under Section 109 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and
Sections 3/25 of the Arms Act, 1959. 
3. While  the  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant(s)  would  submit  that,  though,  the  Government
Advocate was given a very short time, he could not place the
relevant materials before the High Court. The time given was
only for the purpose of assisting the High Court on the issues
raised with respect to the dismissal of the respondent's
discharge application. The High Court, having granted time

--- Page 390 ---
2
only for obtaining instruction, ought not to have passed an
order at the interlocutory stage directing a CBI inquiry.
4. The  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  respondent
submits that the High Court has passed a detailed and reasoned
order after hearing the parties at length. Alternatively, the
learned senior counsel for the respondent stated that in the
event of this Court not being in agreement with the said
submission, the issue pertaining to the CBI inquiry may be
left open to the High Court to be decided at the time of
hearing the criminal revision, finally, one way or the other.
5. Upon hearing the learned senior counsel appearing for the
parties, we are of the opinion that it would be better for the
High Court to decide the necessity of a CBI inquiry while
finally deciding the matter, as what we are dealing with is
only an interim order, pending the main criminal revision
petition.
6. In such view of the matter, the issue pertaining to the CBI
inquiry is left open to be decided by the High Court, after
affording adequate opportunity to the parties concerned. The
observations made in the impugned order, being prima facie, is
expected not to influence the High Court in finally deciding
the matter one way or the other. All the issues are left open.
7. Thus, we also make it clear that we have not expressed
anything on the merits of the case, as it is for the High
Court to pass appropriate orders, as it deems fit.
8. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.

                   Mr. Yashvardhan Shah, Adv.
                   Mr. Ravinder Kumar Yadav, AOR
                                      
        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made 
the following
                      O R D E R
1. The  present  Petition  arises  out  of  the
Impugned Final Judgment and Order dated 03.07.2026
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Chhattisgarh  at
Bilaspur in Criminal Appeal No. 1234 of 2026,
whereby the High Court was pleased to dismiss the
appeal preferred by the Petitioner under Section
14A(2)  of  the  Scheduled  Castes  and  Scheduled
Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. By
the said impugned order, the High Court affirmed
the order dated 30.04.2026 passed by the learned
Special Judge, SC/ST (POA) Act, Mahasamund (C.G.),
rejecting the petitioner’s application for grant
of regular bail. 
2. The Petitioner has been in judicial custody
since  18.03.2026  in  connection  with  FIR  No.
117/2026 registered at Police Station Mahasamund,
SLP (Crl.) No.14518/2026                                                                2

--- Page 401 ---
3
District Mahasamund (C.G.) for offence punishable
under  Sections  296,  64(2)(m),  and  69  of  the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 read with
Sections 3(2)(v) and 3(2)(v)(a) of the Scheduled
Castes  and  Scheduled  Tribes  (Prevention  of
Atrocities) Act, 1989, respectively.
3. We have heard learned counsel appearing for
the  Petitioner  as  well  as  learned  counsel
representing the Respondent-State of Chhattisgarh
and perused the material available on record. 
4. Learned counsel for the Petitioner submits
that the Petitioner and the prosecutrix were known
to each other and the relationship between the
parties was purely consensual, spanning over a
period of almost three years. The dispute arose
upon the breakdown of the relationship, following
which  the  present  criminal  proceedings  were
initiated.  
5. Learned counsel appearing for the Respondent-
State opposed the prayer for bail. We also heard
SLP (Crl.) No.14518/2026                                                                3

--- Page 402 ---
4
the second respondent, the victim, who appeared in
person on video conferencing from the office of
the Superintendent of Police, Mahasamund district.
6. Having considered the submissions of learned
counsel for the parties and having evaluated the
materials placed on record, without expressing any
opinion on the merits of the allegations or the
guilt of the accused, we are of the considered
view that a case for grant of regular bail is made
out,  taking  into  account  the  fact  that  the
Petitioner has been in custody for over four and a
half months, and the trial is likely to take a
considerable amount of time to conclude.
7. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order
dated 03.07.2026 passed by the Hon’ble High Court
of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur in Criminal Appeal No.
1234 of 2026 is set aside. 
8. The Petitioner (Mukesh Patel) is ordered to
be released on regular bail in connection with FIR
No.  117/2026  registered  at  Police  Station
SLP (Crl.) No.14518/2026                                                                4

--- Page 403 ---
5
Mahasamund, District Mahasamund (C.G.), subject to
terms and conditions that the trial court may deem
fit and proper to impose. The petitioner shall
cooperate  with  the  trial  proceedings;  failing
which, the trial court would be entitled to cancel
the bail granted.
9. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly,
disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also
stand disposed of.
(HARPREET KAUR)                   (POOJA SHARMA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 15340 OF 2026]
SANJAY DESHWALI                            APPELLANT
                          VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                 RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R 
1.   Leave granted.
2. By the impugned judgment and order dated 22 nd June, 2026,
the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur has rejected the
appellant’s second application for bail in anticipation of arrest.  
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 0441/2025 dated
15th October, 2025 registered with Police Station-Ayodhya Nagar,
District-Bhopal. It is alleged in the FIR that the appellant has
committed offences punishable under Sections 108, 85 and 3(5) of
the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant as
well as the first respondent-States and the intervenor-complainant.
5. The suicide note of the victim has been perused. We refrain
from making any comment at this stage. 
6. Suffice to note, the appellant was away in Mauritius between

--- Page 422 ---
12th April, 2025 and remained there till 24th December, 2025 whereas
the death by suicide took place on 17 th September, 2025. The
victim’s marriage with the appellant was solemnized in 2012.   Other
family members of the appellant have been granted anticipatory bail
by the High Court.
7. In such view of the matter and considering the nature of
allegations, we are of the opinion that custodial interrogation of the
appellant is not necessary and that there is sufficient ground for the
appellant to be admitted to an order for grant of bail in anticipation
of arrest.
8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set
aside.
9. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
11. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant of
bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
12. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
13.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

[DIPANKAR DATTA]

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
was filed seeking directions to the respondents, including the
Union of India, the Bar Council of India, and the Consortium of
National Law Universities (in short, “Consortium of NLUs”) to
1

--- Page 450 ---
permit the petitioners, who are differently-abled persons, to
appear in the CLAT and AIBE examinations through a computerized
format/mode  and  make  all  necessary  accommodations  for  such
candidates as per the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
and the guidelines issued by the Union of India thereunder from
time to time. 
2. This Court has issued various  interim directions through
orders dated 05.12.2024, 11.12.2024, and 10.02.2026. Finally, on
10.08.2026, it was stated by learned counsel for the Consortium of
NLUs that all the issues raised on behalf of the petitioners will
be effectively addressed before the next examination, which is
likely to be held in December 2026. In that order, we recommended
that  the  Consortium  of  NLUs  evolve  a  comprehensive  Standard
Operating Procedure (SOP) and standing instructions regarding the
issues raised in the instant writ petition.
3. In addition to that, the statement of Ms. Archana Pathak Dave,
learned Additional Solicitor General of India, was also brought on
record to the effect that the revised comprehensive guidelines,
especially  for  enabling  the  persons  with  disabilities  to
effectively participate in the competitive examinations, were in
process and would be finalized after taking suggestions from all
stakeholders. 
4. During the course of hearing today, it was stated by the
learned  Additional  Solicitor  General  of  India  that  the
consultations with respect to the revised policy guidelines to be
2

--- Page 451 ---
issued by the Government of India are now complete and the Union is
in the process of finalising the same.
5. Similarly, the Consortium of NLUs has filed an additional
affidavit  to  the  effect  that  pursuant  to  our  order  dated
10.08.2026, the policy has been updated, and the same is now
available on the website in order to ensure that candidates
similarly-placed as the petitioners are suitably accommodated to
take the CLAT 2027 examination, which is now scheduled to be held
on 06.12.2026. It is further clarified that the updated policy
accounts  for  suggestions  such  as  provision  of  assistance  by
scribe(s),  use  of  assistive  technologies/devices,  as  well  as
appointment of a nodal officer for addressing any other requests
that may be made by the differently-abled candidates. 
6. In light of this and as fairly agreed to by Mr. Amar Jain,
learned counsel for the petitioners, the instant petition is
disposed of in terms of the following directions:
(i) All the interim directions issued by this Court from time to
time are made absolute and shall continue to operate in the future.
(ii) The Consortium of NLUs shall continue to evolve and update the
policy decision to ensure that all facilities are made available to
the differently-abled candidates to facilitate their appearance in
the CLAT examination or any other similar examination.
(iii) The Government of India will, in due course of time, notify
its revised policy guidelines, which shall be meticulously complied
3

--- Page 452 ---
with by the NLUs and all other institutions to facilitate all
differently-abled candidates in competitive examinations.
(iv) The Bar Council of India and the Consortium of NLUs are
further directed to create a grievance redressal mechanism so that
in the event of any difficulty being experienced, the concerned
candidate may approach such authority for redressal. Such mechanism
may include a representative of the candidate(s) suffering from
disability.
7. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION (C) NO(S).29/2025
BHARAT ELECTRONICS LTD. PETITIONER(S)
                              VERSUS
M/S SCHMID TELECOM, ZURICH RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(5) and Section 11 (6)
of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act)
seeks the appointment of a sole arbitrator to adjudicate
disputes  arising  from  the  Technical  Collaboration
Agreement dated 26.06.2020 (Agreement), as subsequently
amended on 30.05.2022, executed between the Petitioner
and the Respondent.
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner, Bharat Electronics
Ltd., is a Navratna PSU under the Ministry of Defence,
Government of India, engaged in the design, development,
and  manufacturing  of  strategic  electronic  equipment,
defence communication systems, and aerospace systems. The
Respondent,  M/s  Schmid  Telecom,  Zurich,  is  a  sole
proprietorship  company  organized  under  the  laws  of
Switzerland, involved in designing, manufacturing, and
marketing IP-based Voice Communication Systems (VCS) for
Air  Traffic  Control.  The  parties  entered  into  the
Agreement dated 26.06.2020 for, inter alia , the transfer
of technology and technical know-how and specialised
engineering  support  to  enable  the  Petitioner  to
indigenously manufacture, test, integrate, and supply
ICAO-compliant IP-based Voice Communication Systems. As
per Clause 20 thereof, disputes between the parties would
1

--- Page 454 ---
be  referred  to  arbitration  in  New  Delhi,  to  be
administered by the International Centre for Alternate
Dispute Resolution (ICADR). 
3. It appears that a dispute arose in 2023, on account
of the alleged failure of the Respondent to meet its
contractual commitments in a time-bound manner, i.e., as
per the agreed milestones. In response, the Respondent
statedly took the position that its performance stood
suspended on account of the non-renewal of an earlier
Memorandum  of  Understanding  dated  03.10.2019,  and
subsequently denied its obligations under the Agreement.
In these circumstances, the Petitioner issued notice
dated 24.02.2025 invoking arbitration. Due to the ICADR
having been statutorily substituted, it was suggested
that  the  Arbitration  be  administered  by  the  India
International  Arbitration  Centre  (IIAC),  New  Delhi.
However, as the Respondent failed to reply to the said
notice, the Petitioner has filed the instant Petition
under Section 11 of the Act.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the Petitioner and
perused  the  material  placed  on  record.  No  one  has
appeared on behalf of the Respondent despite service of
notice through publication. An affidavit of compliance in
this regard has been duly filed by learned counsel for
the Petitioner.
5. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded
above and the relevant provision(s) under the Technical
Collaboration Agreement dated 26.06.2020, as amended on
30.05.2022, we deem it just and proper to allow the
instant Arbitration Petition and appoint Justice Chander
Shekhar, former Judge of the Delhi High Court as the Sole
Arbitrator to resolve the disputes between the parties.
The seat and venue of arbitration, in accordance with the
arbitration agreement, shall be New Delhi, India. Ordered
2

--- Page 455 ---
accordingly.
6. The Arbitrator shall have the liberty to fix his own
remuneration/fees. 
7. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also
stand disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been arraigned as an accused
and seeks regular bail in connection with Cyber
Crime  Case  No.40/2025,  corresponding  to  FIR
No.239/2025 registered at Police Station-Cyber
Crime for the offences punishable under Sections
75,  78,  79,  356(2)  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66(C) and 67 of the
Information Technology Act, 2000.
3. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
1

--- Page 458 ---
the appellant and the learned counsel appearing
for the respondent-State.
4. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant
submits that the punishment provided for the
alleged offence is for a maximum period of three
years, while the learned counsel appearing for
the respondent-State submitted, that considering
the nature of the offence committed, there is no
need for any interference with the impugned
order. 
5. The appellant was working as a Security Guard
and is alleged to have caused damage to the
reputation  through  facebook  post(s)  and
comment(s).  He  has  already  undergone
incarceration for a period of more than one
year. The trial has already commenced. Suffice
it is to state, that the continued incarceration
of the appellant is no longer required. 
6. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
set aside the impugned order passed by the High
Court, and grant regular bail to the appellant.
7. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order  stands  set
aside, and the appellant is granted regular
bail, subject to the terms and conditions that
2

--- Page 459 ---
may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
8. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 16  OF 2026
JIOSTAR INDIA PVT LTD PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
GREEN BEAN SPORTS MARKETING RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The  petition  has  been  filed  under  section  11(6)  of  the
Arbitration  and  Conciliation  Act,  1996  (1996  Act)  seeking
appointment of a Sole Arbitrator for the adjudication of disputes
that have arisen between the parties.
2. The  Petitioner  is  an  Indian  company,  operating  a  leading
entertainment  network,  while  the  Respondent  is  a  company
incorporated in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) dealing with
sports media rights. A Media Rights Sub-License Agreement dated
30.03.2023 was executed between the parties, whereunder the
Petitioner granted the Respondent a sub-license of media rights
in relation to the Indian Premier League (IPL) Seasons 2023 to
2027, exclusively for the territory of Bangladesh. The Agreement
was, thereafter, amended on 01.03.2024. Inter alia, the Agreement
contained a cross-default clause, making defaults under other
similar  agreements  between  the  parties  a  valid  ground  for
termination of the Agreement dated 30.03.2023. As per Clause 27
of the Agreement, the disputes between the parties shall be
determined by a Sole Arbitrator under the 1996 Act, with seat and
1

--- Page 470 ---
venue in Mumbai, India.
3. It is the Petitioner’s case that the Respondent defaulted in
respect of payments under a separate Sub-Licensing Agreement
dated 07.02.2023 relating to broadcasting rights of the Premier
League. Thus, the Petitioner invoked the cross-default clause
under the Agreement dated 30.02.2023 and issued a Termination
Notice,  followed  by  a  Demand  Notice.  The  Respondent  has,
statedly, disputed such liability and failed to clear the same.
4. Hence, the Petitioner invoked the arbitration agreement contained
in Clause 27 of the Agreement and issued an arbitration notice
dated  01.12.2025.  Therein,  the  Petitioner  recommended  the
appointment  of  Mr.  Mikhail  Behl,  Advocate,  as  the  Sole
Arbitrator. The Respondent has not replied to the said notice,
leading to the Petitioner filing the instant Petition.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the Petitioner and perused the
material  placed  on  record.  None  appears  on  behalf  of  the
Respondent, despite service having been completed. 
6. In view of the facts and circumstances recorded above, we deem it
just and proper to allow the instant petition and appoint Justice
S.C. Gupte, former Judge of the Bombay High Court, as the Sole
Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes between the parties arising
out of the Media Rights Sub-License Agreement dated 30.03.2023,
read with the Amendment Agreement dated 01.03.2024. The seat and
venue of the arbitration, in accordance with the said agreement,
shall be Mumbai, India.
2

--- Page 471 ---
7. The Arbitrator shall be at liberty to fix his own fees.
8. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

..........................J.
       (JOYMALYA BAGCHI)

LORVEN ENERGIES INDIA PRIVATE

M/S NEO STRUCTO CONSTRUCTION PVT. 
LTD & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This  petition  under  Section  11  of  the  Arbitration  and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (the 1996 Act) seeks the appointment of a
sole arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising from a Tripartite
Agreement dated 02.12.2020, executed between the Petitioner and the
two Respondent(s).
2. The  Petitioner,  Lorven  Energies  India  Private  Limited
(previously Suaval Lorven India Private Limited), is an Indian
company  specializing  in  insulation  services  for  industrial
facilities. Respondent No. 1, Neo Structo Construction Pvt. Ltd.,
is also an Indian company, whereas Respondent No. 2, Petrofac
International (UAE) LLC, is a company incorporated in the UAE.
Respondent No. 2 was awarded the EPC contract for the MSBP Kochi
Refinery project from Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited and
subcontracted piping and equipment erection work to Respondent
No.1. For the purpose of installation of its equipment, Respondent
No.1 issued Service Purchase Order No. NSC-KL/112/19-20 dated
12.02.2020 to the Petitioner, for a contract value of over Rs. 2.38
crores.
1

--- Page 474 ---
3. It is alleged that although the Petitioner commenced and
carried out the contracted work and duly raised invoices from May
2020, Respondent No. 1 failed to pay the full invoice amounts. In
these circumstances, particularly given Respondent No. 1's stated
financial difficulties, the three parties entered into a Tripartite
Agreement dated 02.12.2020, under which Respondent No. 2 was to
make direct payments to the Petitioner. The Tripartite Agreement
contains  an  arbitration  clause  in  Article  8,  providing  that
arbitration proceedings are to be conducted in New Delhi, in
English, under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
4. It is alleged that despite the Tripartite Agreement, payments
due  to  the  Petitioner  remained  unpaid,  and  the  Respondents,
subsequently, terminated the tripartite arrangement by email dated
20.03.2021, restraining the Petitioner from completing the balance
work. The Petitioner, thus, issued a legal notice dated 04.05.2021,
and approached the MSME Samadhan portal on 01.07.2021, before
issuing a demand-cum-notice invoking arbitration on 23.08.2024.
Since no arbitrator was appointed pursuant to the notice dated
23.08.2024, the Petitioner initially approached the Delhi High
Court for appointment of an arbitrator. However, this being a case
of an international commercial arbitration, that petition was
withdrawn  on  19.12.2025,  and  the  instant  Petition  has  been
preferred.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
2

--- Page 475 ---
6. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision(s) under the Agreement dated 02.12.2020, we
deem it just and proper to allow the instant Arbitration Petition
and appoint Justice Rakesh Kumar Jain, former Judge of the Punjab
and Haryana High Court and former Member (Judicial) of the National
Companies Law Tribunal, as the Sole Arbitrator to resolve the
disputes between the parties. The seat and venue of arbitration, in
accordance with the arbitration agreement, shall be New Delhi,
India. The parties shall be at liberty to raise all the contentions
before the learned Arbitrator.

8. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal No(s). 4620/2026
@SLP (Crl.) No(s). 13842/2026
VISHAL BANSAL                                    Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH                        Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 16.07.2026 passed
by the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla to the extent it
rejects the prayer of the appellant seeking suspension of
sentence awarded by the trial court.
4. On behalf of the appellant it is submitted that there
were three accused including the appellant who were convicted.
Co-accused Yuvraj has been granted bail after suspension of
sentence under order of this Court dated 13.02.2026 whereafter
the other co-accused has been granted bail. However, the
prayer of the appellant was rejected because he did not
surrender after his parole period had expired. It has been
submitted that this is a case based on circumstantial evidence
1

--- Page 478 ---
wherein there is no incriminating recovery from the appellant.
The last seen circumstance is of 25.03.2016 whereas the body
was found after few days. In such circumstances, the last seen
circumstance has very little evidentiary value. Therefore,
the  appellant,  who  has  by  now  suffered  9  years  of
incarceration, is entitled to be released on bail after
suspension of sentence. 
5. The learned counsel for the respondent-State has opposed
the prayer for bail by submitting that besides the last seen
circumstance, there is evidence of conspiracy between the
appellant and other co-accused. Moreover, the appellant had
not surrendered for about 1 year 11 months after expiry of his
parole period. 
6. Be that as it may, without expressing any opinion on the
merits of the pending appeal, we are of the view that the
appellant whose case stands at par with the co-accused Yuvraj
Singh, who has been admitted to bail after suspension of
sentence under order of this Court dated 13.02.2026, is
entitled to the same benefit, particularly when the appellant
has served 9 years of sentence. 
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order of the High
Court rejecting the prayer of the appellant to suspend the
sentence pending consideration of his appeal is set aside. The
sentence awarded by the trial court to the appellant shall
2

--- Page 479 ---
remain suspended pending consideration of his appeal by the
High Court.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as the trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case. The trial court may also
lay  down  some  additional  condition  to  ensure  that  the
appellant does not leave the country.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
    
  
………………………………………………………………..J
[MANOJ MISRA]
………………………………………………………………..J
[VIJAY BISHNOI]
New Delhi;
September 29, 2026.

applicant/petitioner-’Nanda Kishor Rai’.
2. The miscellaneous applications have been filed for
revival of SLP(Crl) Diary No. 33114/2023, SLP(Cr l) Diary
No.22045/2023 & SLP(Crl) Diary No.30352/2023 which were
dismissed  on  02.05.2025.  The  Order  dated  02.05.2025
reads thus:
“Despite dismissal of the applications for
exemption  from  surrendering  filed  by  the
petitioner vide this Court’s order dated 3rd
October,  2023,  the  petitioner  has  not
surrendered. In view of Rule 5 of Order XXII of
the Supreme Court Rules, 2013, the Special Leave
Petitions cannot be entertained. We, therefore,
dismiss the Special Leave Petitions.
If the petitioner surrenders, he can always
apply  for  revival  of  these  Special  Leave
Petitions.
Pending applications also stand closed.”
3. It  is  submitted  by  learned  counsel  for  the

--- Page 486 ---
applicant/petitioner that the applicant/petitioner has
been taken into custody and sent to the Correctional Home
on 11.08.2026. Now he is in custody.
4. In view of the leave granted by this Court that in
the event applicant/petitioner surrenders, he can always
apply for revival of the special leave petitions, we
allow the miscellaneous applications. Consequently, the
dismissal order dated 02.05.2025 of the related special
leave petitions, is recalled.
5. Let the SLP(Crl) Diary No. 33114/2023, SLP(Crl) Diary
No.22045/2023 & SLP(Crl) Diary No.30352/2023  be listed

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petition arises out of the order and
judgment dated 30.01.2023 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay in Writ Petition No. 14547 of 2022,
whereby the chamber summons/application preferred by the
respondent for amendment of the plaint has been allowed.
2. The impugned order passed by the High Court reflects
that the High Court has directed the Trial Court to frame a
specific issue regarding limitation, having regard to the
contention raised that the amendment was sought after a
hiatus of 26 years. The High Court has observed that the
issue relating to delay in filing the chamber summons shall
be framed and adjudicated by the Trial Court along with the
other issues, and all contentions in that regard have been
expressly kept open.
3. Furthermore,  paragraph  6  of  the  impugned  order
reveals that the petitioner had instituted two substantive
suits between the parties, being Suit No. 6907 of 1978 and
Suit No. 536 of 1980. Admittedly, in Suit No. 536 of 1980,
a similar amendment application, which was subject matter
of the present case, was allowed by the court, and the said
order was not challenged.
4. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances, we
do not find any ground or reason to interfere with the
order passed by the High Court. Accordingly, the Special
Leave Petition is dismissed.
2

5. Taking into consideration that the civil suit is of
the year 1978, the Trial Court is requested to expedite the
proceedings and conclude the trial at an early date.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

1. Leave granted.

Act, 1915, has been held  ultra  vires  by the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur,  vide judgment dated 21.04.2025

the aforestated enactment cannot be sustained. The order passed
by  the  High  Court,  confirming  the  confiscation  of  the
appellant’s vehicle under the said provision, is, accordingly,
set aside. 
4. The appellant’s vehicle shall be returned to him within one
week from today under proper acknowledgement.

                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. The petitioner-wife and the respondent no.2-husband are also
present in the Court duly identified by their respective learned
counsel.
3. Though the present petition has been filed by the petitioner-
wife for cancellation of bail granted to the respondent no.2-
husband by the learned SDJM, Bikramganj, Rohtas in connection with
FIR No.119 of 2018 dated 01.06.2018, registered at P.S. Nasriganj,
District Rohtas under Sections 323, 341, 504, 506 and 498(A) of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 and under Section 3/4 of the Dowry
Prohibition Act, 1961 but during the course of the proceedings, the
parties have now agreed that the respondent no.2 would take the
petitioner with him to Assam, where he is working and shall keep
her with him in his house. At this juncture, we note that though
initially, the respondent no.2 was agreeable to take a house on
rent and keep the petitioner in that house but for the present, it
has been agreed between the parties that the petitioner shall live
in her matrimonial home i.e., the place where the respondent no.2
is living in Assam with his mother and she shall not insist on a
separate house.
4. We also note that in terms of our earlier order dated
22.09.2026, the petitioner has come prepared to accompany the
respondent no.2 to Assam.
5. The respondent no.2 has assured the petitioner and has also

--- Page 540 ---
3
taken a stand before the Court that he shall make all efforts to
sort out any differences, which may have existed between his mother
and his wife, the petitioner. It is suggested by learned counsel
for the parties that initially, the Court may give one month time
to the parties to try out this exercise and then depending on the
result, the Court may pass appropriate order on the next date.
6. Having regard to the aforesaid, let the respondent no.2 take
the petitioner to his house to Assam, where the respondent no.2
currently lives with his mother.
7. Though, many issues have been discussed in Court, we do not
want to record the same as ultimately, it is for the parties to
build up a relationship of confidence and trust. We are confident
that the parties being adult, would realise their responsibility
and act in the manner, which is required and expected from them.
8. As jointly prayed for, the matters be listed on 04.12.2026,
retaining its position.
9. On the next date of listing, the Court does not require the
parties to be present physically in the Court, if everything is
well. However, it shall be open for the parties to appear before
the Court, if they desire so, otherwise, learned counsel for the
parties shall convey the position to the Court on the next date of
listing.
10. Interim order passed by this Court on 29.10.2025 to continue
till the next date of listing.

2. The prayer made in the application is that in paragraph
No.4 of the order dated 3rd September, 2026 in Crl.A.No.4210
of 2026, there is a reference to learned counsel for the
appellant which can be interpreted to indicate that he was
restricting his submission for consideration of reducing
the term of sentence to a fixed period. It was submitted
that such observation may be inadvertent and more as a
result of a communication gap, as learned counsel was
prepared on merits and in the alternative, he had further
submitted that at least with regard to the sentence, the
Court may consider reducing the same.
3. Having  considered  the  matter,  we  find  that  the
contention of learned Senior Counsel for the applicant
needs consideration.
1

--- Page 548 ---
4. Accordingly, paragraph No.4 of the order dated 3 rd
September, 2026 in Crl.A.No.4210 of 2026 stands substituted
by:
“4. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
submitted that the sentence is excessively harsh
as it envisages incarceration till the natural
life of the appellant. It is submitted that
Courts have taken a view that such sentence could
not be passed as a matter of course/routine, and
thus the Court may at least consider reducing the
term of sentence to a fixed period, especially
since the appellant has already undergone more
than twelve (12) years and six (06) months of
incarceration.”
5. The present application stands disposed of in the
aforementioned terms.
6. In view of the same, let a fresh order be drawn up.

--- Page 566 ---
2
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO.2729/2026 IN SLP(CRL) NO. 13097/2025
1.  The Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.13097/2025 was filed
by the petitioner seeking grant of bail, arising out of the
impugned order dated 18.06.2025 passed by the High Court of
Uttarakhand at Nainital in Second Bail Application No.81 of 2025.
The said petition was disposed of in the best interest of justice
as well as of the parties vide order dated 01.12.2025 passed by
this Court, pursuant to which the present Miscellaneous Application
No. 2729/2026 has been filed by the applicant/complainant. 
3.  The facts of the case reveals that the petitioner was
absconding for almost 25 years and the Special Task Force (STF) of
the State arrested the petitioner on 23.01.2025 and the trial is
going on.
4. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1-
State of Uttarakhand, at the outset, has stated before this Court
that the State shall take all possible steps to conclude the trial
at an early date.  Learned counsel appearing for respondent No.2
has stated before this Court that the trial is at the verge of
conclusion and the Trial Court be directed to conclude the trial by
holding day to day trial.
5.  This Court after hearing the learned counsel for the parties
is of the opinion that the present miscellaneous application
deserves to be disposed of with a direction to the Trial Court to
conclude the trial as expeditiously as possible preferably within a
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO.2729/2026 IN SLP(CRL) NO. 13097/2025

--- Page 567 ---
3
period of one year and, in case need so arises, the Trial Court
shall also be free to hold day to day hearing of the matter. The
question of granting bail to the petitioner till the conclusion of
trial in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case does not
arise.  
6.  With the aforesaid, the Miscellaneous Application stands
disposed of.
7.  Accordingly, IA No. 211082/2026 also stands disposed of.     
(JAGDISH KUMAR)                                 (KOMAL)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
1

--- Page 629 ---
has  been  filed  seeking  quashing  of  the  interim order  dated
17.09.2026 passed by the Election Commission of India, whereby the
party symbol of the All India Trinamool Congress has been frozen
for the upcoming bye-election.
2. The Election Commission, while passing the impugned order, has
stated in para 39 that in order to place both the rival groups on
an even keel and to protect their rights and interests, and going
by the past precedents, the party symbol has been ordered to be
frozen as an interim order “ till  the  final  determination  of  the
dispute in the matter in terms of para 15 of the Symbols Order.” 
3. Shri Dama Seshadri Naidu, learned Senior Counsel representing
the Election Commission of India as well as learned Senior Counsel
representing the other group were asked to indicate the timeline
within which the proceedings can be completed, and a final order
can be passed by the Election Commission of India.
4. In deference thereto, learned Senior Counsel representing the
Election Commission of India has handed over a chart indicating the
timeline followed in past symbol dispute cases. We are inclined to
rely upon the timeline within which the disputes at serial numbers
3 and 4 of that chart were finally decided.
5. We are informed that pursuant to a notice issued by the
Election Commission of India, the petitioner has already filed its
response, whereas the response from the opposite group is still
awaited. 
6. In such circumstances, we grant four weeks’ time to the
2

--- Page 630 ---
contesting respondents as well as the petitioner to place on record
their additional documents/affidavits/counter affidavits, etc. In
other words, the pleadings shall be completed in all respects
within four weeks. Thereafter, the Election Commission of India
shall take three months’ more time to decide the controversy.
7. Both the groups are directed to extend their full cooperation
to the Election Commission of India.
8. It is further clarified that we have not expressed any opinion
on merits and both sides shall be at liberty to raise their
respective contentions before the Election Commission of India.
9. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
10. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

ITEM NO.24               COURT NO.1               SECTION PIL-W
               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Writ Petition(s)(Criminal)  No(s).  373/2026
ASHWINI KUMAR UPADHYAY                             Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.                              Respondent(s)
Date : 28-09-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay, Adv.
                   Mr. Ashwani Kumar Dubey- 1797, AOR
                   Mr. Nikhil Upadhyay, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner has filed the instant Writ Petition in public
interest seeking varied directions essentially meant to curb the
manufacture and sale of spurious and adulterated drugs and drinks.
The following reliefs have been sought:
“a) direct Union and States to take apt steps to
complete the investigation of fake drug cases within 03
months and trial within 01 year;
b) direct time-bound assessment and confiscation of the
properties  of  fake  drug  manufacturers,  sellers,
financiers & their family members under the PMLA, Benami
Property Act & Black Money Act;
c) direct the Union and States to formulate a SOP for
search, seizure and sampling of adulterated spurious
medicines; and prescribe a timeline for submission of
FSL reports in fake drug cases;
1

--- Page 653 ---
d) direct the Union & States to mandatorily do the
digital recording and videography of search, seizure,
sampling & inventory proceedings;
e) direct Centre to frame a graded sentencing policy to
ensure stringent, proportionate punishment for fake drug
manufacturers & sellers;
f) direct the Law Commission of India to prepare a
report suggesting the necessary changes in existing laws
to prevention fake drugs;
g) direct & declare that Sentence in fake drug cases
shall be consecutive;
h) pass such other orders or directions as Court deems
fit & proper.”
2. To substantiate the issues raised in the Writ Petition, the
petitioner has highlighted the rise in manufacturing, sale, and
distribution of spurious, counterfeit, and adulterated medicines,
injections, and syrups across various States, allegedly resulting
in large-scale casualties and severe organ damage. A reference has
been made to pan-India incidents including contaminated cough
syrups causing deaths of 14 children in Madhya Pradesh, inter-state
fake medicine rackets in Delhi, and supply of counterfeit cancer
drugs across over 90 hospitals in Bengaluru. It is claimed that
over 2 lakh citizens die unnaturally, while 20 lakh citizens suffer
serious illness annually due to these fake medicines.  
3. According to the petitioner, the implementation of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Act, 1940 is impeded by the lack of a uniform
timeline and investigative standards. There is complete absence of
standard  operating  procedures  for  search,  seizure,  digital
recording, and inventory preparation.  
4. Furthermore, the petitioner has contended that properties
2

--- Page 654 ---
acquired through counterfeit drug rackets ought to be confiscated
under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Prohibition of
Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988, or Black Money Act, 2015.
5. We, however, note that the petitioner has not approached the
respondent-authorities before filing the instant Writ Petition. In
such circumstances, where different kind of actions are statedly
required to be undertaken by the respondents, we dispose of this
Writ Petition, without expressing any opinion on merits, with a
direction to the Registry to forward a copy of the Writ Petition to
the respondent-authorities for their consideration. The petitioner
undertakes to deposit the requisite copies of the paper book for
the aforesaid purpose.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

                             O R D E R
1. The  instant  writ  petition,  purportedly  filed  in  public
interest, seeks directions to the Union of India and various State
Authorities to enact a comprehensive legislation against bullying
and ragging in schools. The petitioner himself is stated to be a
minor and is studying in school, and is alleged to have sustained
bullying without any redressal mechanism.
2. We find that this Court has already issued comprehensive
directions to address this issue in Sukdeb Saha v. State of Andhra
Pradesh and Others, 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1515. 
3. That  being  so,  there  is  no  necessity  to  repeat  such
directions. Rather, we deem it appropriate to forward this petition
1

--- Page 1170 ---
as a representation on behalf of the petitioner to the respondents
– Authorities to take appropriate action that may be required in
this matter.

direction to the respondents – Authorities to look into the
grievances raised by the petitioner in accordance with law.
5. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

ITEM NO.24               COURT NO.7               SECTION XII
               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.32829/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 10-07-2026
in WA No.1913/2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Madras]
AIRPORT AUTHORITY OF INDIA                         Petitioner
                                VERSUS
GOLDAIR INDIA PRIVATE LIMITED                      Respondent
FOR ADMISSION 
 
Date : 28-09-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. N. Venkatraman, A.S.G.
                    Mr. Anshul Rai, Adv.
                    Mr. S. K. Pandey, Adv.
                    Mr. Chandrashekhar A Chakalabbi, Adv.
                    Mr. Ojaswa Pathak, Adv.
                    Ms. Mallika Ranjan, Adv.
                    Mr. Raunaq Singh, Adv.
 Mr. Anshul Rai- 3198, AOR
                                                          
For Respondent(s) : Ms. Amrita Narayan, Adv.
                    Ms. Monali Dutta, Adv.
                    Mr. Swastik Dalai- 3926, AOR
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Having heard Mr. N. Venkatraman, learned Additional Solicitor General for
the petitioner and Ms. Amrita Narayan, learned counsel for the respondent, we
are of the considered opinion that no useful purpose would be served by
keeping the special leave petition pending. Though Request for Proposal 1 was
issued as far back as on 21 st October, 2024, grant of concession for ground
handling services at Vijaywada Airport has been stalled for almost two years
1 Tender No.2024_AAI_212075_1
1

--- Page 1174 ---
because of the writ proceedings, which were pending before the High Court, and
where the respondent has now emerged successful in obtaining a declaration
that its technical bid was erroneously regarded as non-responsive; hence, its
financial bid should be considered.
2. We think, it would be in the better interest of all stakeholders including
the public at large if a fresh Request for Proposal is now issued by the petitioner
with simpler and comprehensible terms to obviate any further complication in
future with regard to understanding of what the petitioner precisely requires of
the bidders.
3. We have also borne in mind that no right of any bidder has accrued till
now, which would stand impaired by reason of the order that this Court
proposes to pass as above.

VED PRAKASH @ PAHALWAAN                            Petitioner(s)

IA No. 285049/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
IA No. 285072/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM SURRENDERING WITHIN TIME
 
Date : 22-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : HON'BLE  MR. JUSTICE PRASANNA B. VARALE
                           [IN CHAMBER]
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Sriram P., AOR
                   Mr. Sharang Dhulia, Adv.
                   Mr. Chetan Jadon, Adv.
                   Ms. Shivangi Rajawat, Adv.
                   Mr. Sriram Parakkat, Adv.
                   Mr. Udit Choudhary, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
I.A. No. 285072/2026  
The petitioner prays for an exemption from surrendering. The
material on record shows that the petitioner was convicted by the
Trial Court for committing an offence under Section 307 and was
sentenced to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs.5,000/- with
default clause and other conditions.
The petitioner being aggrieved by the judgment and order
preferred an appeal to the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital.
The learned High Court in a detailed judgment considering the
appreciation of evidence shown by the Trial Court and also by
1

--- Page 1180 ---
recording the independent reasons dismissed the bail by upholding
the conviction and sentence awarded by the Trial Court. Admittedly
the petitioner was throughout on bail. It is the case of the
prosecution that the petitioner was carrying firearms. At this
stage I may only refer to the evidence of PW-6 Dr. Ajay Gupta who
had performed surgery of the brain of the victim and had removed
the fractured bone.
Apart  from  the  testimony  of  the  material  witnesses  the
prosecution also relied on the recovery of certain articles, but
the petitioner is claiming the ground of self defence.
Considering the fact that throughout the trial, the petitioner
enjoyed the liberty and the judgment and order of the Trial Court
convicted the petitioner awarding him sentence is confirmed by the
High Court and there is no substantial ground coming forth to
consider the request for exemption from surrendering.
Accordingly, the application for exemption from surrendering
is rejected.
Petitioner to surrender within a period of two weeks and file
a proof thereafter within a period of four weeks. 
List the matter before the Hon’ble Court.
(PRIYANKA MALIK)                                (POONAM VAID)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             ASSISTANT REGISTRAR

ITEM NO.16               COURT NO.1               SECTION X

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Writ Petition(s)(Civil)  No(s).  1192/2026
SOHANDEB CHATTOPADHYAY                             Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
HONBLE SPEAKER, WEST BENGAL LEGISLATIVE 
ASSEMBLY & ORS. Respondent(s)
Date : 28-09-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Kapil Sibal, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Kalyan Banerjee, Sr. Adv.
                   Ms. Preetika Dwivedi- 2078, AOR
                   Mr. Abhisek Mohanty, Adv.
                   Mr. Ansh Rajauria, Adv.
                   Mr. Anupam Mishra, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
of India seeks a writ of mandamus to the Hon’ble Speaker of West
Bengal  Legislative  Assembly  for  expeditious  adjudication  of
disqualification petition said to have been filed on 08.07.2026
against ten members of the Legislative Assembly, who are impleaded
as respondent Nos. 3 to 12.
2. The facts pleaded are that after the State Assembly elections
in 2026, there was a split in the All India Trinamool Congress and
the private respondents are said to have constituted a rival group
pursuant to an alleged Special Session convened on 22.06.2026. The
1

--- Page 1222 ---
action of the private respondents has been challenged by the
petitioner and some other MLAs through the subject disqualification
petition.
3. It may be noted here that this Court in Keisham Meghachandra
Singh v. Speaker,  Manipur  Legislative  Assembly  &  Ors.,  (2021) 16
SCC  503  has  authoritatively  held  that  while  deciding  a
disqualification petition, the Hon’ble Speaker exercises the power
of a Tribunal and such power is expected to be exercised within a
reasonable period of three months.  
4. In the case at hand, the period of three months will expire on
08.10.2026. We have every reason to believe that the Speaker of the
State Assembly is fully cognizant of the principles laid down by
this Court and will make an endeavor to take an appropriate
decision within reasonable time, in light of the principles laid
down by this Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (supra).
5. The  Writ  Petition  stands  disposed  of  with  pending
application(s), if any.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Ritin Rai, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Gautam Jha, AOR
                   Mr. Dhawal Desai, Adv.                          
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Petitioner-insurer alleges that computation of compensation made by the
High Court in the impugned judgment and order suffers from an error of law
apparent on the face of the record.
3. Such being the grievance, we grant liberty to the petitioner to apply for a
review before the High Court.
4. We make it clear that should the review fail, the petitioner will be at
liberty to return to this Court challenging the order of the High Court impugned
in this special leave petition.
